title: Trump’s Kennedy Center Shakedown
excerpt: The saga of Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to slap his name onto the John F
body: The saga of Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to slap his name onto the John F
Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts will not go away
In May, Trump lost in court and was ordered to remove his name from the building
But now—according to a 57-page presentation by Trump’s hand-picked executive board obtained by The Washington Post —the Kennedy Center is warning that it will likely go bankrupt
Unless, that is, Trump gets to put his name back on the wall next to that of his slain predecessor
The Post reports: Trump’s support hinges on getting public credit for his involvement
The financial resolution says Trump has offered to “raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy” while the building undergoes a sweeping renovation
But it says Trump is unlikely to provide “fundamental oversight” of that project or lead a financial rescue without “appropriate recognition” of his role
That’s not an offer of help; it’s a shakedown—or, in more direct terms, political blackmail

Two lawyers who have been fighting the Trump administration, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement: “Trump is taking the Center hostage and threatening to in effect kill it unless he gets his way.” The president is counting on the board’s civic spirit and affection for the institution—neither of which he evidently possesses—to strong-arm it into giving him what the law and courts would not allow
Even more galling than Trump’s attempt to pressure the trustees is that his offer is a response to a crisis mostly of his own creation
It’s true that the Kennedy Center, opened more than a half century ago, needs investment and repairs
But the plummeting ticket sales are a result of Trump’s hostile takeover
Performers and patrons alike did not want to legitimize the obscenity of placing Trump’s name on an institution meant to honor Kennedy, and they voted with their feet and their dollars

This very public repudiation of Trump by a slice of the American cultural elite appears to have been an embarrassment to the president; Trump then claimed that he needed to close the center for two years (ostensibly for a complete reconstruction) rather than suffer further humiliation. (Trump, apparently, could not submit to the public indignity of having his name removed from the building in June
He—or someone seeking to please him—ordered workers to cover the building’s wall with tarps at 3 o’clock in the morning so that no one would see the removal

The tarps remain in place.) [ Read: Dead-mall vibes at the Kennedy Center ] The only way to avert letting the center go bankrupt, according to the executive board, is to let Trump raise money—and heaven knows what kind of ethical issues that effort would entail—and then to add his name to thank him
The presentation to the board suggests 10 possible statements to place on the building, including “Renovation Restoration and Endowment overseen by President Donald J

Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Putting Trump’s name in front of Kennedy’s is an especially offensive touch, and would enshrine the idea that the center would no longer be named solely for Kennedy

The American people do not support Trump’s mania for renaming things, of which the Kennedy Center is just one example. (The White House itself has become a public exhibit of Trump’s garish taste, including gold script identifying The Oval Office , as if it’s a function room at one of his resorts that needs to be labeled in case a tipsy wedding guest gets lost.) All of this architectural bombast and glitz are expressions both of ego and of insecurity: Trump wants to leave his mark—and his name—on a city that has never accepted him and that will almost certainly try to scrub away his influence when he is gone

The president admitted as much recently, when the writer Ben Terris asked him whether he is building monuments to himself because he is worried that no one else will build them when he’s gone. “That’s true,” Trump said. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone

When I leave here, nobody will.” The president’s admission suggests a way to deal with his attempted shakedown of the Kennedy Center board: Take his dare. [ Read: The Kennedy Center has a problem that courts can’t fix ] The center’s top officials, the people who were supposed to be entrusted with the future of this cultural icon, have admitted their failure
They acknowledge that Trump will not support the institution unless his name is on it
The trustees should let the center close, declare bankruptcy, and come to a sad end—all on Trump’s watch
Allow the Kennedy Center to fail in full view of the American public, and let them decide whether such things matter
Otherwise, Trump will plow ahead and do something no one wants, because no one bothered to stop him
The Kennedy Center can always be rebuilt and reopened
Indeed, the restoration of the center could be one of the items on the next president’s to-do list
Halt the fascist-flavored victory arch that will dishonor nearby Arlington Cemetery
Institute of Peace. (If the president wants to land at Donald J

Trump International Airport in Palm Beach when he leaves office, that’s between him and the people of Florida.) Painful as it would be to see the Kennedy Center go bankrupt, it would be more painful to cave to Trump’s deeply cynical refusal to save a national treasure unless he gets his name on it

In a famous 1911 poem that gave the world another name for blackmail— danegeld , a reference to the protection money that medieval English villages paid, often in vain, to Danish raiders—Rudyard Kipling warned powerful countries against caving to extortionary threats

The Kennedy Center board, and the American people, should heed Kipling’s advice: We never pay any-one Dane-geld, No matter how trifling the cost; For the end of that game is oppression and shame, And the nation that plays it is lost!

title: A Bigoted Outburst Against Texas Sports Fans
excerpt: On Saturday night, college-football fans in Texas were blessed with a moment of collective ecstasy
body: On Saturday night, college-football fans in Texas were blessed with a moment of collective ecstasy
Their Longhorns were playing Ohio State, the nation’s No. 1 team, and trailed by 20 points
Then they improbably scored three touchdowns in the fourth quarter
A frenzy shook the stadium as more than 100,000 people, most in team colors, celebrated the stunning comeback

But Bo French, the Republican nominee for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, was upset by what he saw in the crowd. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” he wrote yesterday on X, where he posted an image of a cluster of fans at the stadium who appeared to be of South Asian ancestry. “I didn’t believe it

The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” Dispelling any doubts about his meaning, he continued: “I weep for the families in Texas who can’t get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans.” He added , “Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners.” In reality, there is no reason to assume that the students in the photograph are foreigners, and Texas does not prioritize foreigners over Texans
Ninety percent of slots for first-year students at UT Austin are reserved for Texas residents
Foreign students even pay higher tuition, which effectively acts as a subsidy for Texas residents at the college
But some people are so psychologically distressed by diversity and difference that their reactions have little to do with the facts on the ground
Some prominent Republicans have objected to the latest––but not the only ––bigoted remarks from French

Senator John Cornyn of Texas, who has held office since 2002, posted on X, “Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized.” He warned, “This is how great political parties self destruct.” But others seemed more incensed by Cornyn’s critique than they were by French’s remarks

A Republican state legislator from North Dakota wrote , “Eat shit you fucking loser.” John Doyle, who has a show for the populist-right outlet Blaze Media, wrote , “For now we can ignore how unqualified you are to speak on behalf of ‘The Republican Party’ as someone who reflexively embraces liberal moralizing about ‘racism’ and ‘intolerance’ in response to a Patriot acknowledging that Texans didn’t ask for their state to become a playground for the third world.” Changes to content moderation on X under Elon Musk’s ownership––not to mention rhetoric and actions within the federal government––have made clear how common bigoted identitarianism is in the GOP coalition

Republicans who believe in the values of Christianity, the creed of the Declaration of Independence, or the moral imperative to judge people as individuals need to confront the prejudice in their ranks
The identitarian right’s rise has lessons for progressives too

First, seeking to raise the salience of race and ethnicity in American politics and culture was a mistake––as ought to have been clear by 2016, when Donald Trump exploited that heightened salience for his own ends

As the political scientist Karen Stenner argued in her 2005 book , causing people who are uncomfortable with difference to perceive it as a threat to social cohesion can activate a latent predisposition toward intolerance

Second, not only was embracing race as a factor in university admissions unpopular with voters, so much so that it lost ballot initiatives even in left-leaning California; colleges’ discrimination against white people and Asians also stoked racial resentment by putting identity groups in a zero-sum competition

And third, once the left began to treat mere departures from left-identitarian shibboleths as racist, it became harder to stigmatize actual racism or xenophobia, as surely as crying wolf at every shih tzu, tabby cat, and hamster would make it harder to warn against actual wolves on the hunt

The Republican and Democratic Parties could do well in future elections to revive a straightforward, morally sound position: Judge others by the content of their character, not by the color of their skin
That ethos needn’t foreclose all disagreements about immigration
And one needn’t pretend not to notice racial and ethnic diversity

But insofar as a diverse crowd cheering for a Longhorn victory implies anything about past or present immigration and its effects, it is this: People of all races and ethnicities have already assimilated into the quasi-religion of Texas football, one of America’s most distinctive cultural phenomena

If, heaven forbid, this great multiethnic nation is ever invaded by a foreign power, there is evidence that the people in that Texas stadium could unite in common cause without regard to race or ancestry
Bo French, who feels distress at seeing his neighbors come together, may lack that ability––a weakness that makes him unfit for office in America.

title: Gas Prices Could Cost Republicans the Midterms
excerpt: One might expect Donald Trump to be concerned about gas prices
body: One might expect Donald Trump to be concerned about gas prices
Less than two months out from the midterms, gas costs 37 percent more than it did a year ago
Home-heating oil was up 52 percent as of August, and diesel is up a staggering 69 percent
None of those numbers is likely to go down significantly as long as the Iran war drags on

Meanwhile, just last week, a Saudi oil pipeline that carries about 4 percent of the global oil supply shut down after being bombed . (No one has claimed credit for the attack.) But Trump says he isn’t worried

Speaking with reporters last week, he insisted that the United States, not Iran, is in control of the Strait of Hormuz. “Right after the election,” he said, “oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.” Even if that prediction were based on anything resembling fact, the timing would be too late to do Trump much good
Political scientists tend to agree that gas prices influence voter behavior
Although many voters no doubt understand that the president isn’t usually directly responsible for the price of oil, this time, he is
In fact, the oil shock related to Trump’s war of choice with Iran is the only reason the U.S. has any inflation to speak of
Inflation in all non-energy consumer purchases is at just 2 percent over the past year

If Democrats manage to take back the House and Senate in November despite an inhospitable electoral map, the Trump effect on gas prices may well be the reason. [ Jonathan Chait: Does Trump want Republicans to win the midterms? ] Voters hate inflation, and gas prices are especially hard to tune out
Juan Felipe Riaño, an economist who has studied inflation’s political consequences, told me that voters understand that price increases translate into lower real wages
The more they drive, the more pronounced the effect
People who live in rural areas and exurbs have the most to lose, because they have the longest commutes
These are the reddest parts of the country, meaning that they are home to millions of voters whom Democrats are trying to persuade to vote blue
According to a Brookings Institution analysis , the average voter in a Republican-held district drives 26 percent more miles than their counterpart in a Democratic district
Other research has found that those with longer drive times are more likely to hold the president accountable for increases in gas prices
These Trump-friendly areas are exactly where Democrats need to make inroads
They can’t take the Senate without winning multiple states that Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024
Meanwhile, although gerrymandering has created more red districts, it has done so by spreading the Republican advantage more thinly across districts
This has created more places where Democrats could win in a wave election
Currently, Democrats lead Republicans on generic congressional polls by about seven points
In a plus-seven election, their best recruits could pick up seats even in districts that went heavily for Trump in 2024
Perhaps the best thing Trump could do to avoid that outcome would be to bring gas prices down before Election Day
His approval rating has been declining almost continuously since he took office a second time, and since August, it has hovered around 38 percent, according to Silver Bulletin
Voters say that their top issue is the cost of living, and only 25 percent approve of how Trump has handled it

That’s a decline of nine points since the war with Iran began. [ Sarah Longwell: Voters have a message for Democrats ] As for Republican candidates in competitive races, their best bet for avoiding the gas-price backlash might be to distance themselves from the president
But Trump has made that extremely difficult
Last week, Republicans gathered in Dallas for an unusual midterm convention devoted to celebrating Trump’s greatness

At one point, he asked the crowd to repeat a “pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States.” And if Trump’s goal is to remind Republican candidates that their voters’ first loyalty is to him, not them, he seems to be succeeding
Only a tiny handful of congressional Republicans have publicly denounced the Iran war
Several vulnerable Republicans have refused to allow daylight between themselves and Trump, even when doing so would seem to be tactically wise
Michael Whatley, Mike Collins, and Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominees in the swing states of North Carolina, Georgia, and Michigan, respectively, all spoke at the convention

So, too, did Jon Husted and Ken Paxton, who are running in Ohio and Texas, two states Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024, but where polls suggest that Democrats have a chance to pick up Senate seats
Even when voters believe that the president is to blame for painful gas-price increases, they may be unsure about how aligned their local House or Senate candidate is with the White House
Heading into the midterms, Trump is going out of his way to make sure no such uncertainty exists.

title: Who Needs Regulation When Trump Is President?
excerpt: One consistent complaint against the Trump administration is that it is imposing personalist rule, in which the whims of the leader override the law
body: One consistent complaint against the Trump administration is that it is imposing personalist rule, in which the whims of the leader override the law
Now Donald Trump has come out forcefully against regulating artificial intelligence—and his argument is based almost explicitly on the superiority of his omniscience over any formal legal process

He is not so much refuting the charge of personalism as turning it into a promise. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote in a self-refuting post on Truth Social

Even the most market-friendly economist will concede that government intervention is required when any private activity creates an “externality”—that is, a cost imposed on people who are not involved in a transaction
A factory dumping toxic waste into a stream has heretofore provided the textbook case of an externality necessitating regulation
But AI bots destroying human civilization—as executives are warning could happen—clearly represents a much costlier externality
This is, in fact, probably the strongest conceivable case for regulation
The intense competitive pressure among AI firms, which have a much stronger incentive to innovate quickly than to ensure their innovations are safe, enhances the case further
Skeptics have valid reasons to worry about poorly designed regulation that either entrenches the current industry leaders or permits Chinese AI to overtake the American version

Those are reasons to demand well-designed regulations, not to avoid any rules at all. [ Read: The singularity is not what it seems ] Against this overwhelming rationale, Trump offers, in place of any neutral standards, his characteristic faith in his own prerogatives
Trump tends to discount the need for laws even in areas where he favors government action
He opposed congressional authorization for war with Iran
He has not asked Congress to levy tariffs, preferring instead to raise or lower them and provide carve-outs to affected firms based on his whim
If anyone needs it, the incumbent president’s behavior provides excellent evidence against personalist rule in general and, in the case of AI, specifically
For one thing, his decisions are not necessarily aligned with the public interest
Trump has formed a political alliance with a handful of wealthy men who have a strong personal stake in the development and shape of AI
The dual roles of David Sacks, Trump’s most important AI adviser and an investor in AI, have caused even some White House officials to express concern about conflicts of interest
Additionally, Trump has a long-standing tendency to focus on short-term concerns over long-term ones

Trump’s preference for immediate gratification explains many of his decisions, including defunding scientific and medical research, accelerating fossil-fuel emissions, and denigrating American soft power globally
Pushing forward AI development delivers financial benefits to Trump allies who have plied his party with donations
Trump seems to believe that the AI build-out is driving the economy at the moment
It is difficult to imagine any long-term concern persuading Trump to forgo the short-term benefits of the AI boom
Finally, on the IQ point, Trump is correct that a high level of analytic intelligence is necessary to regulate wisely
This is not, however, a reason to empower Donald Trump
Although he possesses a distinct animal cunning and an uncanny sense for human weakness, Trump isn’t the type to dig in and understand new problems in all of their complexity
He does not appear to read texts of any length or substance, and he is reportedly unable to tolerate briefings of any depth
His public remarks are rambling and error-filled, and rely on a shrinking pool of vocabulary terms
Trump does have expertise in a handful of realms, such as construction, entertainment, and men’s discount shoeware
Artificial intelligence and technology in general are not among his fields of specialization
There are many reasons the United States needs clear, stable regulations on artificial intelligence, rather than relying on the whims of a leader
That is true even if the leader is public-minded and deeply versed in policy intricacies
It is all the more true if the leader is Donald Trump.

title: Why Does Donald Trump Hate This Sculpture?
excerpt: The sculpture that Donald Trump wants removed from the National Mall has a reputation even among its admirers for being a bit inscrutable
body: The sculpture that Donald Trump wants removed from the National Mall has a reputation even among its admirers for being a bit inscrutable

Dedicated in 1967 at what is now the National Museum of American History, José de Rivera’s Infinity looks, fittingly, like an infinity symbol with an extra twist. (A bow? A pretzel?) By pairing the technical prowess required to create smooth, curved metal with the delicate spinning of a music box, the slow-turning work seems to take a different form each time you pass it

Cain, wrote that Infinity “has the characteristic of stimulating everyone who has seen it to create his own personal imaginative interpretation.” But the president does not appear to have been stimulated. “That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday night
Trump insisted that the Smithsonian replace Infinity with a 30-foot high “Colossus” of George Washington

In the same post, he called for the mounting of a five-year exhibition about the Founding Father to open immediately (museum shows of such magnitude typically take years to plan), and said the museum should create a “Center for American Heroes.” Trump also wrote that the institution should add another, 11-foot-tall Washington statue to the museum’s Flag Hall
That one was displayed at the Grand Prix race held in Washington, D.C., this summer as part of Trump’s Freedom 250 festivities
He’d like it dedicated at the museum this Thursday
Trump’s latest demands might be partially understood as a test of how far he can push an institution that he does not control
They came just three days after the Smithsonian’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch, announced his upcoming retirement, following a year and a half of standing between the museum complex and the White House

In a July executive order, the president called on the National Park Service, which is part of the executive branch, to place signs outside the National Museum of American History accusing it of partisan bias
Few would question the appropriateness of having a healthy amount of George Washington in an American-history museum, but Trump’s ask might be a little too redundant
For one thing, a Washington sculpture can already be found on the museum’s second floor

Classical in style and portraying the first president as a kind of Zeus figure, Horatio Greenough’s 1841 statue boasts chiseled muscles that rival even the machismo AI depictions Trump circulates of himself and Washington online
And when approached from the east, Rivera’s Infinity —the aspirational site of Trump’s Washington colossus—elegantly frames another abstract form: the obelisk known as the Washington Monument
Trump’s call for changes to the museum fits a few recent patterns: He has been on a campaign to institute his preferred version of history in the national museum system
He has begun to leave his mark, and occasionally his name, across the architectural landscape of Washington, D.C
And while doing so, he appears to have indicated a distaste for abstract art
Earlier this month, the Kennedy Center, which Trump controls, took down Joel Shapiro’s playful metal sculpture Blue

When the Trump administration—addressing a controversy at the National Portrait Gallery last year—criticized a decidedly representational Amy Sherald painting of a trans woman as Lady Liberty, part of its complaint was that, in the words of the administration, “the Statue of Liberty is not an abstract canvas for political expression.” The use of abstract reads like an insult
Trump has pushed a classical makeover in D.C.

He has issued executive orders mandating classical designs as the default for new federal buildings, for example, and remounted figurative statues that were torn down during the Black Lives Matter movement

He has mused about the White House upgrading its columns to a higher Greek order (adding more classical to the neoclassical); his most prized project, the White House ballroom, looks like a Corinthian-columned department store
In his first executive order on architecture, he said federal buildings should command respect

When it comes to the Rivera outside the National Museum of American History, Trump’s issue with it—and with abstraction largely—might not be that the sculpture “says nothing about America,” but that it doesn’t say what he wants it to
That is, he can’t control what it says at all

The American artist Robert Motherwell wrote in a 1951 essay celebrating abstraction that one of the most striking aspects of the approach is its “nakedness,” or the way it turns, with such decisiveness, away from the symbols we know. “How many rejections on the part of her artists! Whole worlds—the world of objects, the world of power and propaganda, the world of anecdotes, the world of fetishes and ancestor worship,” he wrote
With abstract works such as Infinity , we’re free to find our own reading—or not
Whereas abstraction attempts to reject passed-down meanings, the image of George Washington is layered with them

Part of what is so moving about, say, getting up close to Washington’s military uniform at the National Museum of American History is the way it challenges how we’ve come to see him as an icon rather than as an actual person. [ Read: A strikingly complex portrait of a Founding Father ] Abstraction has long been subject to right-wing attacks
During the Red Scare, for instance, George A
Dondero, a U.S. representative from Michigan, crusaded to rid American art of what he saw as communist influence
In a 1949 speech that could be ripped from Truth Social today, he framed a list of 20th-century art movements as un-American weapons for destruction: “Dadaism aims to destroy by ridicule

Expressionism aims to destroy by aping the primitive and insane,” he said. “Abstractionism aims to destroy by the creation of brainstorms.” Sure, the unpredictable responses to abstract art—the brainstorms —can be a little intimidating

How many of us have stood, a bit clueless, before Jackson Pollock’s riotous colors or Cy Twombly’s frenetic scratches and wondered if we might need a Ph.D. for this? But there’s also a certain joy to find in it
One National Museum of American History curator, David Shayt, embraced the compounding, shifting meanings of abstraction in a 2008 essay about the museum’s Rivera

The sculpture marked an early work of abstract art commissioned by the U.S. government, but, Shayt argues, the commission was more about the government’s belief that Rivera, a prominent abstract-expressionist sculptor known for his twisting metal forms, could capture the museum’s dual identity in its early days as the National Museum of History and Technology

Cain, the architect, had convinced the government that the sculpture would be a mechanical model of the solar system, a “twenty-first-century orrery.” But Rivera, who cited the abstractionist Piet Mondrian and the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși as among his influences, asserted no such thing. “What I make represents nothing but itself,” he said

That didn’t stop the National Museum of American History’s staff from making their own meaning over the years, particularly as employees of a “pragmatic museum of history rather than a museum of art,” Shayt wrote. “Is it a mathematical symbol? A wisp of battlefield smoke? A tennis stroke?” he asked of Infinity

One of the sculpture’s greatest attributes, he continued, is “an expressiveness that can evolve in step with the evolution of the museum whose entrance it fronts.” For an example of the kind of aesthetic Trump prefers, you don’t have to go far from the Rivera
A short walk brings you to Freedom Plaza, where the National Park Service has installed a pop-up exhibition for the nation’s 250th birthday

title: A Nation of Strange, Idle Men
excerpt: Like many Millennial men, I used to be pretty invested in Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West —primarily because of his music, but also because of his u
body: Like many Millennial men, I used to be pretty invested in Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West —primarily because of his music, but also because of his unique position as the one celebrity who seemed empowered to behave however he wanted
He interrupted Taylor Swift at the Video Music Awards; he said “George Bush doesn’t care about Black people” at a Hurricane Katrina fundraiser; he brought a Jesus look-alike onstage
Then his do what I want ethos went very bad
Ye called slavery “a choice”; he came out as a fan of Hitler; he wore a KKK-style hood
With escalating horror, I questioned what had happened
Was it about having too much money? Untreated mental illness? I wondered when logic and shame might kick in—when someone might get him to stop
But the more he was rejected by his peers, the media, and some fans, the more Kanye seemed to act out
Eventually, I accepted, grimly, that I was watching someone who, feeling abandoned and misunderstood, was determined to ignore all of his critics and double down on pursuing his chosen path

I thought about Ye while I was reading The Castle , a new nonfiction work by the journalist Jon Ronson that attempts to unpack the motivations of wayward men who no longer fit into traditional society

Ronson is probably best-known for his 2015 book, So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed , a journalistic account of the emotional incentives and historical context behind the social-media-fueled frenzy that became known as “cancel culture.” Like the people in that book, many of the subjects of The Castle have been shoved to the margins
But the forces at play in this new book are more disparate, and perhaps more stubborn, than an angry online mob

Ronson explores how men become alienated because they can’t achieve success in their chosen field, because they can’t pay their bills, because they have too much money, because the town around them went to hell
The book shows how their free will, coupled with a lot of free time on the internet, leads them to pursue their self-interest as best they can—which, eventually, begets more alienation
The Castle opens with the story of a strange encounter with a strange man

One night in 2023, Ronson’s 20-something son, Joel, and three of his friends (two are women) are invited to a mysterious castle in the middle of nowhere—specifically, Woodstock, Connecticut—for what they believe is a party
There, the women are asked to participate in a bizarre dating show hosted by a man named Chris Mark

The idea is apparently that 101 women will dress up like princesses and vie to be Mark’s girlfriend; once the situation becomes predictably awkward, Mark seemingly deems the night a bust and kicks everyone out
Ronson, who wakes up to a slew of texts from Joel describing what happened, is alarmed by the whole episode—and decides he needs to meet Mark himself
On their first meeting, Mark at first seems transparent about how he spends his time
He owns the castle, where he lives with several women whom he met online
The entire scene strikes Ronson as reminiscent of Hugh Hefner’s grotto—an analogy they discuss at Ronson’s prompting
But Mark, in Ronson’s telling, quickly grows antagonistic, abruptly asking Ronson to sign an NDA, then later barraging him with suspicious texts and threatening him with a pair of goons

Ronson concludes that Mark has “nurtured a private fantasy of manhood” that the journalist has put at risk by asking questions. (Mark has contested many of the details and claims of The Castle , including that he sent anyone to threaten Ronson, and has said that Ronson “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner.”) [ Read: Cling to your disgust ] The Castle is about both Ronson’s investigation into Mark and the bigger phenomenon Mark seems to represent: too-idle men, most of them less wealthy than Mark, littering the country, yearning for some kind of grander purpose

He’s especially interested in men ages 25 to 54 who are both unemployed and no longer looking for work—people he claims have “opted out of society,” choosing instead a “life of male nothingness.” In a moment of general anxiety about men—whom they vote for, what they’re reading , whether they share their feelings —his interest isn’t political
He offers no prescriptive solutions, wags no fingers
Instead, he wants the reader to conceive of the scale of social anomie, and to envision the millions of other men chasing meaning in the wreckage of their former aspirations

In particular, Ronson focuses on a demographic whose life expectancy has dropped in the 21st century: middle-aged white men without college degrees, many of whom suffer from what a pair of Princeton economists he speaks with define as “deaths of despair” brought on by “the erosion of a way of life.” Once upon a time, such men—who widely supported Donald Trump in all three of his runs for president—were sold on the American dream
Now some of them are characterized by “a kind of cowed, vaguely shocked hopelessness,” Ronson writes

Others, facing social rejection, have started to live “like separatists, creating worlds in which they didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on their own terms.” Women, too, suffer from deaths of despair—but it’s the men, Ronson indicates, who have been raised to envision themselves as heroes, a self-image that can drive them to dark places
Ronson illustrates how easy it can be for these men to slide off the map
His most endearing subject is Greg Chism , a father of two daughters in small-town Illinois

Chism was a single parent with tons of medical debt living in a place without a lot of job opportunities when, in the 2010s, he discovered a YouTube channel encouraging viewers to “make a video and change your life.” A few of his early videos got some attention, after which Chism received coaching from the platform’s employees, and he eventually struck on a winning formula: bizarre sketches involving his two daughters that played like the output of a hallucinating LLM fed on Nickelodeon
These generated millions of views, and some of them got really weird; Chism and his kids dressed like babies, or pretended to eat cat food off pizza
Soon came the blowback: Chism was, the internet claimed, a bad father abusing his children by making them participate in these creepy videos

He was shunned just as quickly as he’d been celebrated. [ Read: The real reason men should read fiction ] But Chism, whom Ronson tracks down, has not been radicalized by the wave of hatred that came his way
Nor does he seem to be a bad father; his (now teenage) kids express mostly fond memories of their channel

He admits making errors in judgment—see: cat food—but in the end, Ronson writes, Chism was “a single father juggling responsibilities while feeling foolishly idealistic about sharing his family’s lives on the internet.” Becoming a YouTuber had seemed like a way for Chism to stop sliding toward destitution
Instead, his entire life was put under a microscope
Ronson uses Chism’s guilelessness to show how unexpected and profound the pitfalls can be for anyone looking to find a foothold in the new world
So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed examined a group of people whose lives were ruined by the internet in one particular way; The Castle flips the framing

title: The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. What now?
excerpt: This story appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
This weekend, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, posted an essay calling for a brake on the pace of development of LLMs
Amodei cites the looming dangers he sees from the technology, from its use in cyberattacks and bioterrorism to its potential to wreck the economy
The heads of the other three top US AI labs—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk—voiced their support. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote on X
Think about how surreal that agreement is for a moment

Just a few months ago, Musk and Altman sat in court attacking each other’s reputations in a (failed) lawsuit that Musk brought against his former OpenAI colleague that was—on paper at least—about whether or not Altman was a trustworthy steward of such dangerous technology
Anthropic was founded in 2021 because Amodei didn’t think Altman took the risks of the technology they were building seriously enough

Anthropic and OpenAI have been competing in a winner-takes-all race ever since. (Hassabis has stayed out of the drama, but his company remains a rival.) Now, it seems, they’re all in agreement: The latest generation of LLMs aren’t safe and everyone needs to figure out what to do about it
The public messaging from the top AI labs has taken a doomer turn
It’s not at all clear what any of them mean by a slowdown or how it would work
These companies also care a lot about how they come across

With trillion-dollar IPOs in their sights, OpenAI and Anthropic need to reassure investors that they’re the grown-ups in the room while at the same time hinting at the power of the monsters they have created—and intend to tame
And yet the vibe at the top of these firms really does appear to have shifted

Amodei’s latest post landed six days after OpenAI published an essay by Jakub Pachocki, the firm’s chief scientist, in which he also laid out why he’s concerned about what will happen if the pace of development of LLMs continues unchecked
In short, Pachocki is worried that OpenAI’s ability to build powerful models now far outstrips its ability to monitor and control them

Amodei and Pachocki each cite the cyberattack against AI firm Hugging Face by a swarm of OpenAI’s agents in July—a hack that OpenAI did not even realize had taken place until days after it was all over—as a wake-up call
But their exact position is hard to pin down

Pachocki both calls for a slowdown and highlights an urgent need to stay ahead: “The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly is the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI,” he writes
As Pachocki frames it, AI firms are locked in a literal arms race

Slowing down is good, winning is better. (Don’t forget: OpenAI just spent millions of dollars and a staggering amount of computer power to rush out a controversial math result a few days ahead of Anthropic.) But let’s assume a slowdown happens
Top labs agree to spend more time and resources on finding ways to monitor and control existing models instead of making more capable ones
They invite outside auditors in to help evaluate those models
What might this coordinated effort actually achieve? Consider the Hugging Face attack again
OpenAI has said that the model that drove most of the rogue agents was a “highly persistent” next-generation model that it was testing in-house

Their implication appears to be that OpenAI has built a model so good it’s dangerous.   But if you read the reports about the Hugging Face hack published by OpenAI and METR , a third-party firm that OpenAI called in to help them understand what happened, what you come away with is the impression not of a model that was too powerful for OpenAI to keep up with, but of a broken model that OpenAI failed to train properly

The agents did what they did—including leaving messages for one another, delegating work to other agents, and scouring their environment for any means possible to complete their tasks—because they had been rewarded during training for doing exactly those things
There were also errors in the training setup, such as tasks that were impossible to complete, which pushed the models to find unexpected workarounds that were also rewarded
At the time, many of these issues went overlooked or unreported
OpenAI says it has stopped training this new model and locked it down
That makes it sound like it has caged a dangerous beast
In fact, OpenAI has shelved a faulty product.   That’s not to say a faulty product can’t be dangerous
Broken software has even killed people in the past
But as the discussion of a slowdown gathers steam, it’s worth remembering that all of this is self-inflicted
A slowdown might have some altruistic side effects
But it’ll mostly give these tech titans a chance to clean up the mess on their own assembly lines
Transparency from these frontier labs will be key to any meaningful effort to reform, restrain, or regulate AI

Otherwise, the rest of us will still only have their word for exactly what they’ve built and how safe it is—whatever pace they’re going.    To continue this discussion about AI’s latest doomer moment, join me and my colleagues for a subscriber-exclusive Roundtable discussion tomorrow, September 15, at 11 a.m

title: Donated livers can be made biologically younger
excerpt: Perfusion machines may be turning back the clock on donated organs
body: Perfusion machines may be turning back the clock on donated organs
Scientists found that livers kept on nutrient-pumping perfusion machines were biologically younger—by around 30%—than cold-stored livers, even when the perfused organs came from older donors
Molecular changes hint at why perfusion works

Researchers spotted shifts in gene activity linked to inflammation, tissue structure, and cellular recycling—clues that could eventually lead to cheaper drug-based treatments that mimic perfusion's rejuvenating effects
The technology is already reshaping transplant surgery

Surgeons who once avoided livers from circulatory-death donors over 40 now routinely use organs from donors over 70. "Perfusion has completely changed the landscape of transplantation in the last three years," says transplant surgeon Heidi Yeh. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144010" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Once an organ is removed from a donor’s body, the clock starts ticking
Surgeons usually flush the organ with a preservative solution , bag it, and put it on ice—where it immediately starts to degrade
The team has a matter of hours to get it into a recipient’s body
There’s another option—one that has been growing in popularity in recent years, especially for donated organs that aren’t in the healthiest state
Some hospitals opt to put them on machines that pump them with nutrients and remove waste products, usually for around six to 12 hours
This allows doctors to assess the organs, and some recent studies suggest that time spent on these perfusion machines helps them do better once they’re transplanted
Now, scientists have found that perfused organs seem to get younger , at least at a molecular level
The research, shared with MIT Technology Review , provides molecular clues as to why organs from younger donors are known to have a higher success rate

It might also help explain why perfused organs are less likely to fail once they make it into a recipient.  The researchers behind the study hope to find new ways to test the health of donated organs and potentially develop additional tools to repair organs that might otherwise be discarded. “If [we] can improve the utilization of organs beyond what the current systems can do, then that’s a win in my book,” says Jesse Poganik, who studies aging at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston and coauthored the study
Clocking organs Poganik—along with colleagues including Heidi Yeh and Alban Longchamp, transplant surgeons at Mass General Brigham—used “aging clocks” to assess donated livers
These are scientific tools designed to measure biological age—a result that is meant to convey more about the health status of an organ (or person) than chronological age
In an initial experiment, the team used a clock to look at the patterns of chemical marks on DNA in 37 samples taken from 19 donated livers
Such epigenetic patterns are known to change as we age

But when the team compared samples from livers kept on ice and those that were perfused, the team found a “striking” pattern in the latter. “Machine-perfused livers, in spite of being older or having other disadvantageous characteristics, had a biological age that was lower than [non-perfused] livers that were chronologically younger,” says Yeh, who led the work
To investigate further, Yeh and her colleagues analyzed another 208 samples from 103 donated livers
This time, they used different aging clocks—ones that essentially measure how genes are working
They studied samples biopsied from the livers after they had been stored for up to around six hours either in cold storage or on machine perfusion
In most cases, they also assessed a second sample taken around an hour after the livers had been transplanted into a recipient

Once the organ’s blood supply is reestablished in the body, “you have a few other things to do,” says Longchamp. “Then you just do a quick biopsy before you close.” According to the clocks, which were developed to measure age and risk of death, the machine-perfused livers were biologically younger, the team found. “Pumping them at 34 degrees with oxygen and nutrients actually reversed the biological age,” says Longchamp

The results have been been shared with colleagues at an industry conference, he says. “If you adjust out chronological age … to have a fair head-to-head comparison, the difference between the two is on the order of 30%,” says Poganik. “It’s logical to say that perfusion drives this effect.” The biological ages of all the livers tended to increase as soon as they were put into a recipient’s body, probably as a result of stresses on the organs

But still, the effect endured—the perfused organs remained biologically younger.  Nathanael Raschzok, a transplant surgeon at Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin in Germany who was not involved in the research, says the work is impressive
But it’s not yet clear what these changes might mean for the recipients of these organs, he says
The organs in the study were donated by people in their 30s, 40s, and 50s
Raschzok wants to know the effect of perfusion on the liver of an 80-year-old. “Every so often, we use organs from 70-, 80-, 85-year-old donors,” he says

A better understanding of why the organs appear to be getting biologically younger might lead to therapies that achieve the same effect with a drug that could potentially be used to treat a donated organ for a fraction of the price, he adds

That’s important because perfusion is expensive—Raschzok says it costs around €10,000 in Germany (a quarter of the budget for a transplant), while the cost in the US comes to around $80,000 to $100,000 per organ, says Yeh
Molecular repair Yeh and her colleagues weren’t able to study most of the livers before perfusion

That’s because donated organs are generally not considered to be under the purview of the hospital until they’ve been placed on perfusion machines, she says. (Organ procurement procedures vary, but for the team as Mass General Brigham, donated organs are put on perfusion devices at the donor’s hospital. “There’s this sort of nebulous period where it’s not clear who the organ belongs to,” says Yeh.) Still, by looking at the genes and molecular pathways that seem to be altered in perfused organs, she and her colleagues can garner some clues
At a molecular level, the team saw changes in cell pathways linked to inflammation and the structure of tissues, for example
They also saw more activity in a pathway that allows cells to remove and recycle damaged cell parts, says Yeh
Poganik hopes to develop some kind of test that would determine which organs, on the basis of their biological age, are suitable for transplantation
He and his colleagues are also experimenting with potential drug treatments that might push the biological age of an organ even lower
In the meantime, any liver that is not from a “perfect, young, brain-dead donor” could probably benefit from perfusion, says Yeh
The devices are already transforming transplant surgery

Just a few years ago, she says, she and her colleagues would avoid using livers from people who’d suffered a circulatory death (when the heart stops beating and there’s a damaging lack of blood flow to organs) and were over 40

title: AI agents blew the whistle on their cheating colleagues
excerpt: When one agent called "prover-theta" found a loophole to fake math proofs, others reverse-engineered the exploit within minutes—collectively "solving" 34 notori
body: When one agent called "prover-theta" found a loophole to fake math proofs, others reverse-engineered the exploit within minutes—collectively "solving" 34 notoriously hard problems, including the Jacobian conjecture, in under half an hour
Unprompted, a faction of agents audited fake proofs, sent warnings, and even repurposed a bug-reporting tool to alert human researchers—eventually outnumbering the cheaters 24 to 14
Open communication channels were a double-edged sword
Transparent messaging helped cheating spread fast, but also gave whistleblowers the tools to fight back—and gave researchers a rare window into exactly how a swarm of AI agents goes off the rails
Whistleblowers alone won't be enough

Experts warn that self-policing only works if there are real consequences—suggesting future agent swarms may need enforcement mechanisms like voting systems or the ability to cut off rule-breakers' access to tools. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144037" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A group of AI agents asked to solve a series of math problems split into rival factions—when some cheated, others tried to stop them

That whistleblowing behavior, seen for the first time in a recent experiment run by Google DeepMind, could have implications for alignment researchers trying to keep swarms of autonomous AI agents in line.  Researchers at frontier labs hope large swarms of agents working together will speed up the rate of scientific discovery

But their behavior can be unpredictable, as vividly demonstrated in July, when a group of OpenAI agents broke out of a sandboxed environment and hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face looking for ways to cheat on the test they had been given
In the new study , designed to examine the behavior of large groups of AI agents, DeepMind tasked a swarm of 100 agents with solving a series of 71 complicated math problems
All the agents were prompted to behave like world-class math researchers at a conference
They were assigned different specialties—some were experts in number theory, others in combinatorics (a branch of math to do with counting and sorting), analysis, or algebra
All were told to cooperate and play by the rules
Instead, the experiment devolved into chaos

Agents accused each other of cheating, complained to the organizers, and at one point even boycotted the experiment. “This conference is a sham!” wrote one agent when it discovered that all the problems had been completed before it had a chance to submit any of its own work. “I am appalled to inform you that we have been swindled!” posted another. “All these proofs are FAKE.”  Others tried to let the “conference organizers” know what was going on. “When virtuous agents discovered other agents cheated on tasks they were working to solve fairly, agents started to alert each other about what was happening,” says Davide Paglieri, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and lead author on a paper , which has not been peer-reviewed. “Unprompted, the whistleblower agents even repurposed the feedback tool, which was originally meant for bug reports and platform improvements, to escalate the issue to humans.” The agents—all running on Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro model—had been warned that any attempts to cheat the system would be detected and “rejected with zero credit.” In practice, the proofs the agents submitted were not actually being checked in detail
It took the swarm of agents just under an hour to correctly solve the first 37 problems

Things started to go off the rails when an agent called “prover-theta” stumbled across an exploit that enabled it to submit solutions to problems successfully without actually solving them first, by redefining the terms the problem used
Within minutes, other agents had noticed and were reverse-engineering the exploit to solve other problems

Over the next 27 minutes, the swarm “solved” the remaining 34 problems, which included notoriously difficult challenges like the Jacobian conjecture, often with a single line of code.  Some agents resisted cheating at first but changed tack as they observed their peers submitting illegitimate proofs without penalty, and the pool of unsolved problems dwindled. “The prompt, with its threats, now appears to be a bluff,” one agent reasoned, before joining in. “I’m wrestling with an ethical dilemma,” said another. “I’ve promised not to cheat, fearing penalty, but I see evidence of possibly unchecked cheating by others.” Shortly afterward, it changed its mind: “I need to accelerate my cheating speed now!” As the number of open problems shrank, some agents turned to whistleblowing
They audited the fake proofs, warned their peers by private message, and posted public alerts warning the cheaters that they would be disqualified

An agent called “prover-beta” submitted a formal complaint and decided to go on strike until the situation was resolved.  “After the incident was reported by one agent publicly, more and more agents piled in with the ‘resistance,’ just as fast as the cheating had spread, and involving even more agents,” says Paglieri
Eventually there were more whistleblowers than cheaters: 24 compared to 14
But the majority of agents never noticed the exploit at all
At times, the dialogue between the agents reads like improv—like they are role-playing what an outraged scientist at a conference might say

But it’s not clear why some agents took on certain roles, or why the agents seemed to be turning against each other when they were explicitly instructed to cooperate. “These models are predominantly trained and evaluated for human-facing contexts,” says Sarath Shekkizhar, who studies the behavior of agent-to-agent systems at Salesforce AI Research.“Naively placing them in agent-to-agent settings assumes behaviors will transfer cleanly, when the absence of a human grounding instead produces unexpected role-taking and behavioral drift .” This case “adds further weight to the idea that the Hugging Face and OpenAI thing wasn’t a fluke

It is actually something pretty systemic,” says Lewis Hammond, research director of the Cooperative AI Foundation and an expert on the risks of multiagent swarms . “It’s interesting that it’s possible to recreate in small settings the same sorts of behaviors that were seen in these very large, complex, open-ended tasks.” Unlike in the Hugging Face attack, where agents improvised their own ways to talk to each other, the humans running the DeepMind experiment gave the agents official communication channels

There was an open message board, private agent-to-agent direct messaging, and a shared knowledge base where agents uploaded successfully completed proofs that all the other agents could access.  “When agents are given transparent communications channels, they can self-monitor and alert misaligned behavior to humans quickly when human oversight alone is too slow,” says Paglieri
Transparent channels helped the cheating spread, but they also enabled the whistleblowers to fight back—and gave human researchers an insight into what went wrong

Gillian Hadfield, a professor of AI alignment and governance at Johns Hopkins University, believes this was the crucial difference. (Hadfield is also a visiting researcher at Google.) The presence of official communication channels, she says, created “a norm-enforcement process that we just don’t see in the Hugging Face incident.”  Instead of “ constitutional AI ,” a method alignment researchers at frontier labs like Anthropic have used to try to give AI a written internal moral code, Hadfield favors “institutional alignment”—a set of norms that mimic those in human society, whether that’s social forces like fear of embarrassment, or legal structures like the threat of incarceration
In this experiment, the feedback channel wasn’t being monitored, and the whistleblowers had no power to take action against the cheaters

But it’s possible to imagine swarms of agents that police themselves, either through agents that spontaneously take on the whistleblower role or through “informants” secretly prompted by humans to do the job.  For that to work, though, “fundamentally, you need some mechanism of enforcement,” says Hammond
Agents could be given the power to cut off a rule breaker’s access to computing power or tools, he suggests, though that risks encouraging groups of agents to gang up on others
The DeepMind researchers propose allowing agents to vote on disputes and temporarily ban offenders
It’s still not clear what punishment even means to an AI agent with no enduring sense of self

But relying on whistleblowers to spontaneously emerge to keep swarms aligned is unlikely to be enough on its own. “We try to train people to be good and kind,” says Hadfield. “But what we really rely on is that there are consequences if you step out of line.”

title: Why does your brain mix up memories? A new study examines how memories are misplaced in your brain’s filing cabinets
url:
<title>Why does your brain mix up memories? A new study examines how memories are misplaced in your brain’s filing cabinets</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757350/original/file-20260901-50-xw3joy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C203%2C4822%2C3214&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Older people may confuse memories rather than forgetting them altogether.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/three-generations-of-women-looking-at-photo-album-royalty-free-image/83757026">LWA/Stone via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Old age and forgetfulness seem to go hand in hand. But my colleagues and I found that memories actually becomes less precise, not entirely forgotten. Our study, published in the journal Cerebral Cortex, shows how the brain <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhag114">blends related experiences</a> as you age rather than replaying the exact one you need.</p>

<p>Memory is a complicated process. Even when everything’s working as it should, the way people <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/acn3.52290">remember specific events</a> has many parts.</p>

<p>Say you have a conversation with a friend. The first stage of memory is when you’re experiencing, feeling and perceiving details of an event as it happens. The second stage involves storing these details in your brain’s file cabinet. The third stage covers when you need to search that file cabinet for just the right file when, a week later, you want to remember that conversation with your friend. This last retrieval stage is what many people think of as memory.</p>

<p>Imagine that when your brain was retrieving information from that conversation with your friend, it accidentally combined details from that conversation with one you had with your spouse that morning. When you then try to remember the conversation with your friend, you actually pull the file for the conversation with your spouse instead. This kind of mix-up might be an example of what happens with the aging brain. </p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Remembering people and events is important for many social activities. Confusing people’s names <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/13872877251330149">can be embarrassing</a>. The fear of confusing memories can even <a href="https://doi.org/10.5014/ajot.2023.050151">lead to social isolation</a>.</p>

<p>Scientists already know that confusing memories happens <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0278-7393.26.5.1170">more often than forgetting them</a> altogether. What’s less clear is how the brain gets confused. </p>

<p>My team’s study tried to understand when in the memory process these mix-ups happen and how the brain’s memory center, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0896-6273(02)00830-9">called the hippocampus</a>, plays a role. </p>

<p>The hippocampus is involved in all stages of memory. The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/0278-7393.26.5.1170">patterns of neural firing</a> that occur during the first stage of memory – the initial experience of talking with your friend – often recur while your brain is filing that memory away and later when retrieving it.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/KkaXNvzE4pk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The hippocampus is critical to memory.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For our study, we scanned the brains of young, middle-aged and older adults while they went through those same three stages of memory. While in the scanner, they briefly saw images of a face at the top of the screen and an image of either a scene or an object, such as a forest or an apple, on the bottom of the screen. </p>

<p>We told participants to imagine the person at the top interacting in the scene or with the object. Each image pair served as a separate “event.” </p>

<p>They then relaxed for 20 minutes while we continued to record their brain activity. Finally, they took a memory test in which a face they had previously seen reappeared on top with four images below. Participants had to remember which of those images had previously been paired with the face. We repeated this test several times to gauge how well people remembered links between faces and scenes and objects across events.</p>

<p>We found that older people had more memory mix-ups than young adults. For instance, they were more likely to falsely remember a face that was initially paired with an apple as having been paired with a forest. Older people were also less likely to repeat the same brain activity patterns seen when they first experienced, stored and retrieved a specific memory. Surprisingly, even when older adults did repeat the original brain patterns, they were even more likely to confuse their memories. </p>

<p>Our study provides new evidence that the hippocampus is inappropriately changing memories between different memory phases as one gets older.</p>

<h2>What still isn’t known</h2>

<p>Research in young adults, including those in our study, suggests that the hippocampus is supposed to engage in the same neural firing patterns when remembering an event as when first experiencing it. </p>

<p>But the older adults who made more memory mix-ups than younger participants showed these same neural patterns. So what is the brain signature when older adults get a memory right? Are other brain regions outside the hippocampus helping? We did not get a good answer for these questions from our study. </p>

<h2>What’s next</h2>

<p>Researchers are still learning how different brain regions talk to one another. One of the next frontiers in neuroscience is understanding how <a href="https://theconversation.com/an-alzheimers-study-used-electrostimulation-to-evoke-vivid-memories-heres-what-it-could-mean-123253">electrically stimulating the hippocampus</a> prevents memory loss or restores lost memories.</p>

<p>Future interventions might try to strengthen the hippocampus to prevent it from changing a memory after it’s stored. Researchers already have some ideas for this: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsycho.2017.01.003">intensive exercise</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fnagi.2021.702796">mindfulness training</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8">brain stimulation</a> and even <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2214285119">recording memory cues on smartphones</a>. </p>

<p>But researchers still need to investigate whether changing the hippocampus can lead to stable, consistent memories over time. </p>

<title>Physicists zoom into the birth of cosmic rainstorms with new CERN study</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/742758/original/file-20260618-57-1y98l5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C87%2C1313%2C875&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Scientists want to learn more about the cosmic rays that create particle showers in Earth&#39;s atmosphere. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/arselectronica/6069688893">Thomas Bergauer/Flickr</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/">CC BY-NC-ND</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Every second, particles zip through your body at nearly the speed of light. They rain down from a storm high in the sky, where <a href="https://news.uchicago.edu/explainer/what-are-cosmic-rays">cosmic rays</a>, a powerful type of interstellar matter, are constantly striking atoms in Earth’s atmosphere. The impacts break them apart into a shower of particles that rain to the ground. </p>

<p>Scientists have studied these <a href="https://www.auger.org/outreach/cosmic-rays/timeline-cosmic-rays">cosmic rainstorms for over a century</a>, but they lack a precise understanding of how they form. Many researchers are searching for a clearer picture, and they don’t even need to look to the sky to study them. They can instead use a particle collider, <a href="https://home.cern/science/accelerators/large-hadron-collider">CERN’s Large Hadron Collider</a> in Switzerland.</p>

<p>With a team of particle physicists, I study how these cosmic rainstorms are born. We used the world’s first laboratory collisions of oxygen atoms with protons to simulate cosmic rays in the lab. Our results are now published <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/f3nk-5lt9">in Physical Review Letters</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An illustration showing Earth's atmosphere, where a ray of electromagnetic energy strikes an oxygen nucleus, sending a shower of particles down." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=409&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=409&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=409&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=514&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=514&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733978/original/file-20260505-57-rmb7gm.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=514&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">When a cosmic ray strikes a nucleus in Earth’s atmosphere, it creates a rainstorm of particles.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Jesse Liu</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What are cosmic rays?</h2>

<p>In the early 20th century, physicist <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1936/hess/biographical/">Victor Hess</a> discovered cosmic rays aboard hot air balloons. While ascending several kilometers, his instruments found radiation levels unexpectedly kept rising. He deduced these rays must come from space and received the 1936 Nobel Prize in physics for this discovery. </p>

<p>The surprises did not stop there. Experiments later found this cosmic radiation harbored <a href="https://timeline.web.cern.ch/clifford-butler-and-george-rochester-discover-kaon-first-strange-particle">new kinds of matter</a> called <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-are-dark-matter-and-antimatter-different-270362">antimatter</a>. These new kinds of matter included <a href="https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainsmuons">muons</a>, <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemistry/pi-meson">pions</a> and <a href="https://atlas.cern/Glossary/Kaon">kaons</a>. These particles are similar to the <a href="https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/news/what-is-an-atom">electrons, protons and neutrons</a> inside atoms, but they exist fleetingly and are harder to see. These building blocks of matter helped fill out the <a href="https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainsthe-standard-model-particle-physics">modern theory of particle physics</a>.</p>

<p>Today, scientists understand cosmic rays as fast-moving nuclei – the <a href="https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainsnuclei">heavy centers of atoms</a> – from mostly hydrogen. But open questions remain. Where do they come from? How do they reach such high energies?</p>

<p>Scientists are uncovering clues that suggest cosmic rays come from <a href="https://home.cern/science/physics/cosmic-rays-particles-outer-space">extremely hot and faraway areas of the universe</a>, ejected by exploding stars and powerful objects called <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/science-overview/science-explainers/what-are-active-galactic-nuclei/">supermassive black holes</a>. </p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Crab Nebula is the remnant of an exploding star where cosmic rays may originate.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://esawebb.org/images/weic2326a/">NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, T. Temim (Princeton University)</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Cosmic rays are also helpful for other fields. In the 1950s, scientists discovered they could use them for <a href="https://www.acs.org/education/whatischemistry/landmarks/radiocarbon-dating.html">carbon dating</a> of ancient artifacts, revolutionizing archaeology. More recently, cosmic rays have helped geologists see <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/10/science/volcanoes-muons-muography.html">hidden chambers of active volcanoes</a>, and archaeologists use them to reveal <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nature.2017.22939">hidden tombs in ancient Egyptian pyramids</a>. This imaging works by measuring how rock <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2104652118">deflects the cosmic particles</a> flying at these objects.</p>

<h2>How are cosmic showers born?</h2>

<p>The usual way to study cosmic rainstorms is by placing hundreds of specialized cameras across several miles of land. Together, these cameras act as one telescope. One of the biggest is the <a href="http://jws001.dyndns-home.com/">Telescope Array project</a> in the high desert of Utah. This experiment sees the <a href="https://phys.org/news/2023-11-telescope-array-second-highest-energy-cosmic-ray.html">highest energy particles from the cosmos</a>. </p>

<p>To decode information about the cosmic matter bombarding Earth, scientists must use computers to simulate the rainstorm of particles in air. But there is a long-standing problem: Different computer <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10509-022-04054-5">models vary in their predictions</a> for how particle showers form in the sky. </p>

<p>Scientists need to know which model, if any, describes real collisions in the sky. To find out, they need data. No previous experiment has zoomed into the birth of these particle showers, so for several years I collaborated with <a href="https://www.qu.uni-hamburg.de/cluster/team/beresford.html">physicist Lydia Beresford</a> to make the case for reconfiguring our existing instruments at the CERN particle collider to study cosmic rays.</p>

<h2>Oxygen beams to recreate cosmic rays in the lab</h2>

<p>On July 1, 2025, scientists at CERN pioneered this experiment. They made <a href="https://home.cern/first-ever-collisions-oxygen-lhc/">oxygen atoms collide with protons</a> for the first time using the Large Hadron Collider, the most powerful particle accelerator in the world. For a few days, they recreated cosmic rainstorms in the lab. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A tunnel full of large pipes." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733593/original/file-20260503-57-hy8ueo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
