            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In this new experiment, a proton beam acted as the cosmic ray, while the oxygen beam played the role of Earth’s atmosphere. The energy in each collision converted into a spray of particles, recreating the first moments of a cosmic rainstorm. </p>

<p>At the <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-large-hadron-collider-gets-reset-and-refreshed-each-year-a-cern-physicist-explains-how-the-team-uses-subatomic-splashes-to-restart-the-experiments-229227">Large Hadron Collider</a>, several particle cameras take photos of collisions. One of these cameras that I work on is <a href="https://atlas.cern/Discover/Detector">called the ATLAS experiment</a>. This giant instrument is the size of a football field, which thousands of scientists work together to run. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://atlas.cern/Discover/Detector/Inner-Detector">high-speed camera at the heart of ATLAS</a> can take over 200 million photos in a day. It uses a large set of silicon sensors to take close-up portraits of particles, similar to the sensors in your phone camera.</p>

<h2>First close-up photos of cosmic rainstorms</h2>

<p>Along with a small team of physicists, we analyzed these images and used the photos to measure both how many particles the collisions created and at what energies they flew out from the collisions. We were able to measure the properties of these particles over 10 times more precisely than what computer models predicted. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A diagram showing two particles colliding and sending off a shower of other particles in an underground tunnel." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=359&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=359&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=359&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=451&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=451&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/733552/original/file-20260501-71-1k0dyc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=451&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Image captured by the ATLAS experiment of a collision between a proton and oxygen nucleus that recreates a cosmic rainstorm of particles in the lab shown as the yellow lines.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PAPERS/STDM-2025-08">CERN/ATLAS Collaboration</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our results will help pinpoint how many high-energy cosmic rays are made of hydrogen, compared to heavier atoms. Understanding their composition could provide important clues about their origins. We were excited to share such valuable data. So we promptly sought feedback from experts in the ATLAS collaboration, then received the green light to <a href="https://agenda.infn.it/event/48435/contributions/287691/">go public</a> <a href="https://home.cern/atlas-acts-cosmic-ray-laboratory/">with our results</a>. </p>

<p>Our study renews the links between particle physics and high-energy astrophysics. Both fields have lots of overlap and shared history, but they remain separate fields, with much to learn from collaborating with each other. My colleagues and I hope these results will improve scientists’ knowledge of cosmic rainstorms and help unravel the most extreme events in the universe.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/280890/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Scientists want to learn more about the cosmic rays that create particle showers in Earth's atmosphere
Thomas Bergauer/Flickr , CC BY-NC-ND Every second, particles zip through your body at nearly the speed of light
They rain down from a storm high in the sky, where cosmic rays , a powerful type of interstellar matter, are constantly striking atoms in Earth’s atmosphere
The impacts break them apart into a shower of particles that rain to the ground
Scientists have studied these cosmic rainstorms for over a century , but they lack a precise understanding of how they form
Many researchers are searching for a clearer picture, and they don’t even need to look to the sky to study them
They can instead use a particle collider, CERN’s Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland
With a team of particle physicists, I study how these cosmic rainstorms are born
We used the world’s first laboratory collisions of oxygen atoms with protons to simulate cosmic rays in the lab
Our results are now published in Physical Review Letters
When a cosmic ray strikes a nucleus in Earth’s atmosphere, it creates a rainstorm of particles
Jesse Liu , CC BY What are cosmic rays? In the early 20th century, physicist Victor Hess discovered cosmic rays aboard hot air balloons
While ascending several kilometers, his instruments found radiation levels unexpectedly kept rising
He deduced these rays must come from space and received the 1936 Nobel Prize in physics for this discovery
Experiments later found this cosmic radiation harbored new kinds of matter called antimatter
These new kinds of matter included muons , pions and kaons
These particles are similar to the electrons, protons and neutrons inside atoms, but they exist fleetingly and are harder to see
These building blocks of matter helped fill out the modern theory of particle physics
Today, scientists understand cosmic rays as fast-moving nuclei – the heavy centers of atoms – from mostly hydrogen

Where do they come from? How do they reach such high energies? Scientists are uncovering clues that suggest cosmic rays come from extremely hot and faraway areas of the universe , ejected by exploding stars and powerful objects called supermassive black holes
The Crab Nebula is the remnant of an exploding star where cosmic rays may originate
Temim (Princeton University) , CC BY Cosmic rays are also helpful for other fields
In the 1950s, scientists discovered they could use them for carbon dating of ancient artifacts, revolutionizing archaeology
More recently, cosmic rays have helped geologists see hidden chambers of active volcanoes , and archaeologists use them to reveal hidden tombs in ancient Egyptian pyramids
This imaging works by measuring how rock deflects the cosmic particles flying at these objects
How are cosmic showers born? The usual way to study cosmic rainstorms is by placing hundreds of specialized cameras across several miles of land
Together, these cameras act as one telescope
One of the biggest is the Telescope Array project in the high desert of Utah
This experiment sees the highest energy particles from the cosmos
To decode information about the cosmic matter bombarding Earth, scientists must use computers to simulate the rainstorm of particles in air
But there is a long-standing problem: Different computer models vary in their predictions for how particle showers form in the sky
Scientists need to know which model, if any, describes real collisions in the sky

No previous experiment has zoomed into the birth of these particle showers, so for several years I collaborated with physicist Lydia Beresford to make the case for reconfiguring our existing instruments at the CERN particle collider to study cosmic rays
Oxygen beams to recreate cosmic rays in the lab On July 1, 2025, scientists at CERN pioneered this experiment
They made oxygen atoms collide with protons for the first time using the Large Hadron Collider, the most powerful particle accelerator in the world
For a few days, they recreated cosmic rainstorms in the lab
The Large Hadron Collider introduced oxygen beams for the first time in 2025, accelerated to nearly the speed of light
Maximilien Brice/CERN , CC BY In this new experiment, a proton beam acted as the cosmic ray, while the oxygen beam played the role of Earth’s atmosphere
The energy in each collision converted into a spray of particles, recreating the first moments of a cosmic rainstorm
At the Large Hadron Collider , several particle cameras take photos of collisions

title: Wildfire strategy doesn’t need a winner – with 3 camps fighting for dominance, the system can’t keep up with the risk

<title>Wildfire strategy doesn’t need a winner – with 3 camps fighting for dominance, the system can’t keep up with the risk</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759189/original/file-20260910-50-myfnwu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=39%2C0%2C6141%2C4094&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A firefighter monitors a backfire in California, set to clear away dry vegetation that could fuel wildfires.  </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/forest-service-firefighter-monitors-backfire-during-the-news-photo/2165259858?adppopup=true">Josh Edelson/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>One of the problems with how America deals with wildfires is thinking there is one primary strategy that can end the nation’s wildfire crisis. Whether that’s <a href="https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/07/07/californias-wildfire-defense-blasts-off-governor-newsom-launches-firesat-wildfire-detection-satellites-to-spot-blazes-from-space/">detecting</a> and <a href="https://www.eenews.net/articles/burgums-wildfire-mandate-smother-every-blaze/">putting out every fire fast</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/boosting-timber-harvesting-in-national-forests-while-cutting-public-oversight-wont-fix-americas-wildfire-problem-264097">increasing logging and forest thinning</a>, or <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab2356">allowing fires to burn under safe conditions</a>, the default choice today is to pour more money and effort into the star approach of the moment. </p>

<p>But effective wildfire strategy in the face of <a href="https://www.nifc.gov/">worsening fire seasons</a> demands a system of actions – interconnected pieces that reinforce one another.</p>

<p>Right now, those pieces mostly are not connected. Research groups, governments and organizations tend to separate into distinct camps, each promoting its own specific strategy. The <a href="https://www.weforum.org/publications/from-wildfire-risk-to-resilience-the-investment-case-for-action-2026">result is a system that can’t keep up</a> with the rising fire risk.</p>

<p><iframe id="IIyG4" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/IIyG4/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="How much land burns each year in wildfires"></iframe></p>



<p>Our team of researchers, along with fire ecologist Jim Menakis, who recently retired from the U.S. Forest Service, has been looking at wildfires from social, ecological and risk-science perspectives to help forest and fire managers and communities in fire-prone areas turn research into practices that can reduce fire-related risks.</p>

<p>We have seen the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/jofore/fvy020">pitfalls</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.350.6263.920-b">of current</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/jofore/fvad036">fire management approaches</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1071/WF21168">also</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s44391-025-00038-4">examples</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08941920.2022.2092803">of</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08941920.2022.2092803">what</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s44391-025-00038-4">actually</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ropr.12379">works</a>.</p>

<h2>Three separate camps</h2>

<p>Wildfire strategy tends to break into three distinct camps today, each focusing heavily on one approach over the others.</p>

<p>One camp wants to <a href="https://www.fs.usda.gov/inside-fs/leadership/2026-fire-letter-intent">double down on suppressing</a> every ignition quickly and aggressively, contending that it’s the surest way to prevent immediate loss. The direction to put out every fire quickly has been a <a href="https://theconversation.com/big-fires-demand-a-big-response-how-1910s-big-burn-can-help-us-think-smarter-about-fighting-wildfires-and-living-with-fire-167317">foundation of the U.S. government response</a> to wildfires since the early 1900s, and persists <a href="https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/pmb/owf/upload/1995-Federal-Fire-Policy.pdf">despite attempts over the years to change it</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A firefighter stands on a burned landscape, with smoke still rising" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759191/original/file-20260910-50-o0sagt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A firefighter stands on a burned area in steep, rugged mountains near Big Sur, Calif. Fires are natural parts of the landscape and can clear out excess brush, but letting them burn, unless they’re carefully managed fires, is rarely considered.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/firefighter-stands-on-the-burnt-area-the-plaskett-fire-news-photo/2292616270?adppopup=true">Wai Lee Michael Ho/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A second camp says the real problem is fuel: flammable vegetation that has been piling up for decades in forests and rangelands due to too much fire suppression. </p>

<p>This group’s solution is to scale up forest and brush thinning through logging and controlled burning. Calls for these actions span political administrations, from the U.S. Forest Service’s <a href="https://www.fs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/Wildfire-Crisis-Implementation-Plan.pdf">Wildfire Crisis Strategy</a> during the Biden administration to the Trump administration’s 2025 executive order calling for the <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/03/immediate-expansion-of-american-timber-production/">expansion of American timber production</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-trumps-plan-to-rescind-the-roadless-rule-protecting-national-forests-will-struggle-in-court-290496">rescinding protections for roadless areas</a> of national forests. But while excessive fuel is a problem, particularly during dry periods, it isn’t the only issue.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A Forest Service staff member points to an area of thinned trees amid a forest. All the trees are several feet apart, the forest floor is most clear of vegetation, and there is an open space." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=491&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=491&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759192/original/file-20260910-50-e021cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=491&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A U.S. Forest Service staff member points to a patch of forest where the trees were removed to thin the amount of vegetation. The area in the background was clear-cut as a break to help slow fires.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/forest-service-silviculturalist-amy-krommes-walks-through-a-news-photo/2074741?adppopup=true">Kevin Moloney/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A third camp says fire is coming regardless, and people <a href="http://doi.org/10.1038/nature13946">have to live with it</a> by accepting and promoting more fire, but <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab2356">allowing it to burn on our terms</a>, when and where it’s safe. This is often called managed wildfire. It sometimes includes <a href="https://forestsandrangelands.gov/documents/strategy/natl-cohesive-wildland-fire-mgmt-strategy-addendum-update-2023.pdf">creating landscapes and communities</a> that can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1617464114">survive and recover from fire</a>.</p>

<p>Each camp tends to operate in isolation of the others, often with its own budget, workforce, practices and cultures. These silos can inhibit communication and coordination, <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/fire4030041">which can make fire management less effective</a>.</p>

<h2>Success stories at the intersections</h2>

<p>The question for fire management shouldn’t be “which of the three is right?” It should be “where do they reinforce each other?”</p>

<p>Successful fire strategies combine many approaches to lower the risk. If you look closely, you can see some of the ways these methods intersect.</p>

<p>Fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning of vegetation and thinning forests,  used in the right locations, don’t stop fires on their own, but they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-025-00369-0">can make suppression safer and more effective</a> by lowering a fire’s intensity.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A row of firefighters with a hose and a line of fire across grasslands." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759193/original/file-20260910-50-mz2q1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Firefighters practice their skills while conducting a prescribed burn to remove dry, flammable vegetation that could fuel intense, destructive fires. Prescribed burns can also make fighting future fires there safer.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/marin-county-firefighters-train-during-a-prescribed-burn-on-news-photo/2282119356?adppopup=true">Heather Diehl/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://cfri.colostate.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2023/12/Beeton_etal_Using_Improving_Pods_2319.pdf">Using prescribed burns and forest thinning strategically</a> can also make it safer for managers to allow lower-intensity fire to expand under favorable weather conditions, thereby dampening future fire risk and letting fire <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s42408-022-00139-2">play its ecological role</a> in renewing natural systems. A fire meant to spread still needs a safe edge to stop at, and fuel treatments serve this purpose.</p>

<p>And while suppression and the idea of living with fire appear to oppose each other, the same <a href="http://doi.org/10.1080/08941920.2022.2092803">detection and real-time decision tools</a> that let crews hit a fire hard and fast are exactly the tools needed to allow a fire to burn under safe conditions. Living with fire becomes credible only after fuel treatments have lowered risk to communities.</p>

<h2>A place where everyone is working together</h2>

<p>Wildfire activity has <a href="http://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms8537">increased markedly</a> across many parts of the U.S. in recent decades, resulting in <a href="http://doi.org/10.1029/2020rg000726">destruction to communities</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2011048118">harm to water supplies</a> and tragic fatalities. We believe that changing this trajectory requires a shift in thinking, from promoting a single “best” wildfire strategy to designing stronger connections between strategic options.</p>

<p>Building these connections has to begin long before a fire starts, continue while the fire burns and <a href="http://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02165-9">endure long after the fire has ended</a>. It includes how fire research and fire-risk-reduction projects are designed and funded, how communities are brought into planning to build trust and support, and <a href="https://wildfirerisk.org/">how communities can lessen their vulnerability</a> to wildfires, such as home hardening, developing escape routes and updating land use codes.</p>

<p>Reducing fire risk isn’t solely the responsibility of a single government agency or private entity; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1071/WF21168">all sectors of society must contribute</a>.</p>

<p>This is already happening where people are willing to do the hard work.</p>

<p>For example, the <a href="https://nocofireshed.org/">Northern Colorado Fireshed Collaborative</a> brings together federal and state agencies, local governments, water utilities and residents. They coordinate on reducing flammable vegetation across land ownership boundaries, prepare homeowners and communities through education and financial assistance for wildfire prevention measures, and organize response and recovery efforts as one connected system rather than separate ones.</p>

<h2>Everyone has a role</h2>

<p>The wildfire problem exceeds what any single entity can effectively tackle on its own.</p>

<p>Fire scientists, government agencies and local communities all play a role, which means you do, too. Check if your area has a fire collaborative or community wildfire protection plan. Show up to public meetings to stay informed, and start making an impact at home by clearing dry brush around your property and helping neighbors do the same.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lZ3ZQeC7VZQ?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Communities also have a role by reducing fire risk around homes, including home hardening. CalFire.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The path to better strategies is built by people working together, not by policy on a page.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291343/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: A firefighter monitors a backfire in California, set to clear away dry vegetation that could fuel wildfires
Josh Edelson/AFP via Getty Images One of the problems with how America deals with wildfires is thinking there is one primary strategy that can end the nation’s wildfire crisis

Whether that’s detecting and putting out every fire fast , increasing logging and forest thinning , or allowing fires to burn under safe conditions , the default choice today is to pour more money and effort into the star approach of the moment
But effective wildfire strategy in the face of worsening fire seasons demands a system of actions – interconnected pieces that reinforce one another
Right now, those pieces mostly are not connected
Research groups, governments and organizations tend to separate into distinct camps, each promoting its own specific strategy
The result is a system that can’t keep up with the rising fire risk
Our team of researchers, along with fire ecologist Jim Menakis, who recently retired from the U.S

Forest Service, has been looking at wildfires from social, ecological and risk-science perspectives to help forest and fire managers and communities in fire-prone areas turn research into practices that can reduce fire-related risks
We have seen the pitfalls of current fire management approaches and also examples of what actually works
Three separate camps Wildfire strategy tends to break into three distinct camps today, each focusing heavily on one approach over the others
One camp wants to double down on suppressing every ignition quickly and aggressively, contending that it’s the surest way to prevent immediate loss
The direction to put out every fire quickly has been a foundation of the U.S. government response to wildfires since the early 1900s, and persists despite attempts over the years to change it
A firefighter stands on a burned area in steep, rugged mountains near Big Sur, Calif
Fires are natural parts of the landscape and can clear out excess brush, but letting them burn, unless they’re carefully managed fires, is rarely considered

Wai Lee Michael Ho/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images A second camp says the real problem is fuel: flammable vegetation that has been piling up for decades in forests and rangelands due to too much fire suppression
This group’s solution is to scale up forest and brush thinning through logging and controlled burning
Calls for these actions span political administrations, from the U.S

Forest Service’s Wildfire Crisis Strategy during the Biden administration to the Trump administration’s 2025 executive order calling for the expansion of American timber production and rescinding protections for roadless areas of national forests
But while excessive fuel is a problem, particularly during dry periods, it isn’t the only issue
Forest Service staff member points to a patch of forest where the trees were removed to thin the amount of vegetation
The area in the background was clear-cut as a break to help slow fires

Kevin Moloney/Getty Images A third camp says fire is coming regardless, and people have to live with it by accepting and promoting more fire, but allowing it to burn on our terms , when and where it’s safe
It sometimes includes creating landscapes and communities that can survive and recover from fire
Each camp tends to operate in isolation of the others, often with its own budget, workforce, practices and cultures
These silos can inhibit communication and coordination, which can make fire management less effective

Success stories at the intersections The question for fire management shouldn’t be “which of the three is right?” It should be “where do they reinforce each other?” Successful fire strategies combine many approaches to lower the risk
If you look closely, you can see some of the ways these methods intersect

Fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning of vegetation and thinning forests, used in the right locations, don’t stop fires on their own, but they can make suppression safer and more effective by lowering a fire’s intensity
Firefighters practice their skills while conducting a prescribed burn to remove dry, flammable vegetation that could fuel intense, destructive fires
Prescribed burns can also make fighting future fires there safer

Heather Diehl/Getty Images Using prescribed burns and forest thinning strategically can also make it safer for managers to allow lower-intensity fire to expand under favorable weather conditions, thereby dampening future fire risk and letting fire play its ecological role in renewing natural systems
A fire meant to spread still needs a safe edge to stop at, and fuel treatments serve this purpose

And while suppression and the idea of living with fire appear to oppose each other, the same detection and real-time decision tools that let crews hit a fire hard and fast are exactly the tools needed to allow a fire to burn under safe conditions
Living with fire becomes credible only after fuel treatments have lowered risk to communities

A place where everyone is working together Wildfire activity has increased markedly across many parts of the U.S. in recent decades, resulting in destruction to communities , harm to water supplies and tragic fatalities
We believe that changing this trajectory requires a shift in thinking, from promoting a single “best” wildfire strategy to designing stronger connections between strategic options
Building these connections has to begin long before a fire starts, continue while the fire burns and endure long after the fire has ended

It includes how fire research and fire-risk-reduction projects are designed and funded, how communities are brought into planning to build trust and support, and how communities can lessen their vulnerability to wildfires, such as home hardening, developing escape routes and updating land use codes
Reducing fire risk isn’t solely the responsibility of a single government agency or private entity; all sectors of society must contribute

<title>School choice proponents say it offers families more options – but those don’t always extend to immigrant students</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759154/original/file-20260910-60-w7mlcs.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">School choice gives families options, but not all families necessarily have the same ones. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/choice-of-future-profession-royalty-free-image/1450184099?phrase=school%20choice%20&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Andrii Yalanskyi/iStock via Getty Images Plus </a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://baynews9.com/fl/tampa/news/2026/05/27/debate-over-school-choice-heats-up-after-florida-education-association-files-lawsuit-">Educators</a>, <a href="https://www.k12dive.com/news/senators-debate-how-school-choice-harms-or-helps-public-schools-vouchers/810759/">politicians</a> and <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/nyc-charter-school-funding-rally/">education observers</a> have long debated school choice. </p>

<p>This <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/education/education-choice-policy-resources">controversial policy approach</a> lets families pick alternatives to their assigned neighborhood public schools and, in some cases, <a href="https://www.edchoice.org/school-choice/">allows them to use government funds</a> to pay for private school tuition or other educational expenses.</p>

<p>Some of the school choice debate has focused on whether <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/k12/articles/understanding-charter-schools-vs-public-schools">charter schools</a> – meaning publicly funded, independently operated schools – offer students more <a href="https://civilrightsproject.ucla.edu/reports/choice-without-equity-charter-school-segregation-and-the-need-for-civil-rights-standards/">equitable educational opportunities</a> and better academic outcomes than traditional public schools.</p>

<p>Not much of the debate has focused on how school choice can affect immigrant students.</p>

<p>We are scholars of <a href="https://charleston.edu/school-education/faculty/mccorkle-william.php">social studies education</a> and <a href="https://charleston.edu/school-education/faculty/lloyd-beth.php">educational foundations</a>. </p>

<p>In our <a href="https://journal-mobilityhumanities.com/aims-and-scope/information/">forthcoming research</a>, we examined the impact of school choice on the academic outcomes of immigrant students, primarily from low-income families. </p>

<p>We found that school choice often leaves them behind, as they struggle to succeed academically in often less-than-ideal educational environments. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map of South Carolina shows various people standing across it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759156/original/file-20260910-50-gldu2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/south-carolina-us-state-population-map-large-royalty-free-illustration/2186558800?phrase=immigrants%20south%20carolina&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Ivan Burchak/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A study of Charleston schools</h2>

<p>From 2024 through 2025, we analyzed the impact that school choice is having on immigrant students in our city, Charleston, South Carolina. </p>

<p>Though South Carolina’s <a href="https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2025/08/21/s-c-foreign-born-residents-reach-historic-high-level/">foreign-born population</a> is smaller than it is in some states, it has increased by <a href="https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2025/08/21/s-c-foreign-born-residents-reach-historic-high-level/">more than 900%</a> since 1980.</p>

<p>Approximately <a href="https://censusreporter.org/profiles/05000US45019-charleston-county-sc/">7.2% of the residents in Charleston County are foreign-born</a>.  </p>

<p>School choice and the rise of charter and magnet schools can heavily influence immigrant students’ experiences in Charleston schools. </p>

<p>As in many parts of the country, charter schools <a href="https://scdailygazette.com/2026/02/09/growth-of-sc-charter-schools-outpaces-traditional-senators-say-it-needs-more-accountability/">have expanded</a> across Charleston since 1996, <a href="https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t59c040.php">when lawmakers first allowed them in the state</a>. </p>

<p>In 2025, <a href="https://www.wcnc.com/article/news/politics/south-carolina-politics/south-carolina-private-school-vouchers-2025/275-801da2c8-492c-42fb-81d4-c8021ac6131b">South Carolina passed</a> a bill <a href="https://www.scstatehouse.gov/sess126_2025-2026/bills/62.htm">that allows many state residents to use virtual vouchers</a> – or, as they are also called, educational scholarship funds – that people use to pay for scholarships at private schools or, in some cases, to cover <a href="https://www.postandcourier.com/politics/sc-unbundlers-homeschoolers-voucher-program/article_049037b0-b91f-4626-8b5e-afdba9d8de4c.html">home-schooling expenses</a>. </p>

<p>Charter schools have <a href="https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci9030205">increased inequality</a> and <a href="https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1171677.pdf">racial and socioeconomic inequality within</a> school systems, some research shows. </p>

<p>In our opinion, this new voucher plan will <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/3-waves-of-school-vouchers-a-history-of-expansion-and-exclusion/">likely exacerbate</a> these issues. </p>

<p>Another challenge in Charleston is the rise of magnet schools.   </p>

<h2>Magnet schools and inequality</h2>

<p>Magnet schools are <a href="https://magnet.edu/about/what-are-magnet-schools">free, public schools</a> that are often specialized in their scope, and they admit students from a range of neighborhoods. </p>

<p>Magnets, similar to charter schools, can be completely separate schools with their own buildings, or housed within a particular section of a traditional public school. </p>

<p>Unlike charter schools, magnet schools often, but not always, determine prospective students’ acceptance based on certain academic criteria, including how well they score on <a href="https://amhs.ccsdschools.com/about-us/admissions">standardized testing and the student’s GPA</a>. Other magnet schools select students based on a lottery.</p>

<p>Magnet schools, whether at the elementary, middle or high school level, tend to <a href="https://www.edweek.org/leadership/magnet-schools-struggle-to-be-diverse-says-study/2015/06">attract students</a> from wealthier homes and draw particularly white populations. </p>

<p>One reason is that admission to magnet schools – including <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/charleston-county-school-district/academic-magnet-high-school-17566">Academic Magnet High School</a>, Charleston County’s top public high school – is typically based on test scores.</p>

<p>It is often more difficult for students from low-income families, including some immigrant students, to score well on the tests and qualify for these schools. </p>

<p>Since high-performing magnet schools tend to enroll the most privileged students and experienced staff, other nearby public schools might experience drawbacks, like <a href="https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/research/underachieving-and-underenrolled-chronically-low-performing-schools-post-pandemic">decreased enrollment</a> and more <a href="https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED498833.pdf">staff turnover</a>. </p>

<h2>A sharp divide</h2>

<p>Just about a mile from Academic Magnet is North Charleston High School, a traditional public high school that is required to enroll any local resident. </p>

<p>The school has about <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/charleston-county-school-district/north-charleston-high-school-17568">830 students</a>, a number smaller than are actually zoned for the school. <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/charleston-county-school-district/north-charleston-high-school-17568">It also</a> has some of the highest rates of poverty and lowest test scores in the state.</p>

<p>Many students in the area instead attend <a href="https://www.thepeoplesentinel.com/stories/school-choice-is-expanding-for-south-carolina-families,106158">charter schools</a>, magnet schools or even other traditional public schools that <a href="https://www.postandcourier.com/archives/poor-schools-still-on-losing-end-of-choice-group-of-education-leaders-assists-north-charleston/article_e7f31244-78e1-5c85-b074-bbbd606770d9.html">perform better academically</a>, <a href="https://www.ccsdschools.com/family-resources2/student-transfer">which these students can often attend</a> – if they have their own transportation. </p>

<p>This dynamic often creates various challenges for students who remain at struggling neighborhood schools. These issues include worse <a href="https://ocpathink.org/post/independent-journalism/new-research-finds-school-choice-students-outperform-peers">student academic performance</a>, reduced <a href="https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-turnover-united-states-report">teacher retention</a> and increased <a href="https://www.buffalo.edu/news/news-releases.host.html/content/shared/university/news/ub-reporter-articles/stories/2026/07/kimmelberg-school-choice.detail.html">racial and socioeconomic segregation</a>.  </p>

<h2>Our findings</h2>

<p>In our forthcoming study, we examined the academic performance and demographics of three Charleston area schools: <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/charleston-county-school-district/north-charleston-high-school-17568">North Charleston</a>, <a href="https://amhs.ccsdschools.com/">Academic Magnet</a> and <a href="https://fdhs.ddtwo.org/">Fort Dorchester</a>, a <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/dorchester-02/fort-dorchester-high-school-17602">neighborhood public</a> high school. </p>

<p>Approximately 92.5% of the students at North Charleston are Black or Hispanic. </p>

<p>About half the students at Fort Dorchester are Black or Hispanic. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, only 8.9% of the students at <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/charleston-county-school-district/academic-magnet-high-school-17566">Academic Magnet</a> are Black or Hispanic.</p>

<p>Approximately 100% of the students at <a href="https://www.usnews.com/education/best-high-schools/south-carolina/districts/charleston-county-school-district/north-charleston-high-school-17568">North Charleston</a> are economically disadvantaged, meaning they qualify for <a href="https://www.usnews.com/media/best-high-schools/best-high-schools-technical-appendix.pdf">free or reduced lunch</a>. This compares with 60% of students at Fort Dorchester and 13% at Academic Magnet.</p>

<p>While 39.7% of the teachers at North Charleston <a href="https://ed.sc.gov/educators/recruitment-and-recognition/critical-need-areas/crit-need-schools-retirement-25-26/">left after three years</a>, 18.6% of teachers left during this time frame at Fort Dorchester, and another 13.8% at Academic Magnet.</p>

<p>We wanted to examine how these schools’ academic and demographic differences affect immigrant students and their academic performance. </p>

<p>We found that <a href="https://ed.sc.gov/data/test-scores/state-assessments/access-test-scores/">English language proficiency among non-native English-speaking students</a> at North Charleston was 3.4%. Overall, approximately 9.3% of students there had a <a href="https://wida.wisc.edu/sites/default/files/resource/Performance-Definitions-Receptive-Domains.pdf">level 4</a> or higher English language score, out of a total six possible points. </p>

<p>At Fort Dorchester, the numbers were much higher: 16.9% of non-native students were proficient in English, and and overall, 34.4% were at level 4 or above in English.</p>

<p>At Academic Magnet, due to the lack of non-native English speakers, no data was available.</p>

<p>We also interviewed some of the teachers in the “left behind” schools like North Charleston in the district. One shared that immigrant students or children of immigrants started having issues, like skipping school or engaging in disruptive behavior, that they saw other kids doing in these schools.</p>

<p>As one teacher said: “I try to get them to understand, this is not all America … I would just feel so bad for that.” </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three young people walk down a school hallway, as seen from behind." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759159/original/file-20260910-59-dig8nc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Immigrant students do not necessarily experience some of the potential benefits of school choice.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/male-and-female-students-walking-in-corridor-royalty-free-image/2148293018?phrase=%20high%20school%20student%20in%20hallway%20&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Klaus Vedfelt/Digital Vision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Broadening school choice conversations</h2>

<p>We believe that school choice discussions should include immigrant students and magnet schools. In the often-tense discussions on school choice, public school advocates often see magnet schools in a <a href="https://nextstepsblog.org/2016/07/teachers-unions-evolved-magnet-schools-can-charters/">positive light</a>. </p>

<p>However, our study indicates that school choice can often lead to greater segregation and inequality. School choice proponents often laud the benefits of those who use it, but they rarely discuss those who are left behind.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289117/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759344/original/file-20260911-50-f3t40z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Thousands of Jewish and Israeli Americans participate in the annual Israel Day on Fifth parade on May 31, 2026, in New York City.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.es/detail/fotograf%C3%ADa-de-noticias/thousands-of-jewish-and-israeli-americans-fotograf%C3%ADa-de-noticias/2279093114?adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Haverford, a small liberal arts college in Pennsylvania, has become <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/quick-takes/2026/08/10/haverford-settles-antisemitism-lawsuit">the latest U.S. school to settle a lawsuit</a> over how it handled allegations of antisemitism. In a <a href="https://www.haverford.edu/president/news/message-president-raymond-0">statement on Aug. 7, 2026</a>, its president, Wendy Raymond, wrote that “all students including those who identify as Jewish, and/or Israeli, and those who support Zionism: that is, the right of the Jewish people to self-determination and statehood in the land of Israel, are welcome and enjoy equal access to the College and all of its educational programs and activities.” </p>

<p>This statement <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/education/4845135-nyu-clarifies-antisemitism-policies-antizionism/">is not unusual</a>. After the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the start of Israel’s war in Gaza, the United States saw a wave of <a href="https://acleddata.com/brief/us-student-pro-palestine-demonstrations-remain-overwhelmingly-peaceful-acled-insight">campus protests against Israel</a>. Those protests led to a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/nov/05/university-anitisemitism-investigations">surge of complaints about campus antisemitism</a>, and numerous lawsuits and <a href="https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-educations-office-civil-rights-sends-letters-60-universities-under-investigation-antisemitic-discrimination-and-harassment">federal civil rights investigations</a>. </p>

<p>Most of these allegations concerned the alleged mistreatment of Jewish students and faculty who identify as Zionists, or merely <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/jewish-groups-university-california-system-anti-semitism-lawsuit/700918/">refuse to denounce Zionism</a>. That has led some administrations, such as Haverford’s, to explicitly affirm that it is forbidden to harass or otherwise discriminate against students who support Zionism – since such behavior has become <a href="https://www.brandeis.edu/cmjs/antisemitism/antisemitism-prejudice-campus.html">increasingly common on some campuses in recent years</a>.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.international.ucla.edu/israel/person/2520">a scholar of Israel studies</a> who teaches about Zionism, what strikes me when I read such statements is how narrowly they define it, reducing Zionism to a single belief in “the right of the Jewish people to self-determination and statehood in the land of Israel.” </p>

<p>This ignores the fact that there are <a href="https://unpacked.media/theres-no-one-way-to-be-a-zionist-six-different-types-of-zionism/">multiple “Zionisms</a>,” rather than a singular “Zionism,” and that the term has more than just one meaning. It is, at best, oversimplified to describe Zionism only as the belief in the right of Jews to have a Jewish state.</p>

<h2>What do Zionists believe?</h2>

<p>To be sure, this is how <a href="https://www.jta.org/2026/02/04/ideas/the-zionism-gap-what-data-really-shows-about-jews-israel-and-zionism-today">mainstream American Jewish organizations define Zionism</a>. The vast majority of Jewish Americans also think that the “right of the Jewish people to have a Jewish state” <a href="https://www.jewishdatabank.org/api/download/?studyId=1277&amp;mediaId=bjdb%5cJFNA_2025_Survey_of_Jewish_Life_since_October_7_-_Zionism_Release.pdf">is a Zionist belief</a>, according to a March 2025 survey by the Jewish Federations of North America.</p>

<p>Nearly 9 in 10 American Jews said <a href="https://www.jewishdatabank.org/api/download/?studyId=1277&amp;mediaId=bjdb%5cJFNA_Survey_4_IsraelZionismInsights.pdf">they believed that Israel has the right to exist</a> as a Jewish and democratic state. Yet only around a third identified as Zionists. Why, then, do these Jews not consider themselves Zionists?</p>

<p>This may be because many Jewish Americans think Zionism includes other beliefs, too – beliefs that they do not share. For example, <a href="https://www.jewishdatabank.org/api/download/?studyId=1277&amp;mediaId=bjdb%5cJFNA_2025_Survey_of_Jewish_Life_since_October_7_-_Zionism_Release.pdf">in the same survey</a> around a third thought that “Believing Israel has a right to the West Bank and Gaza Strip” is part of Zionism. Around a quarter believed that “Supporting whatever actions Israel takes” is also part of Zionism. </p>

<p>They are not necessarily wrong. Reducing Zionism to a single abstract principle ignores the fact that it is a <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/Z/bo43636872.html">diverse ideology</a> that has changed over time and become the official ideology of the state of Israel. </p>

<h2>A changing ideology</h2>

<p>Since modern Zionism emerged in the late 1800s, it has included <a href="https://jps.org/books/the-zionist-ideas/">many different ideas</a> about Jewish identity, history, politics, culture and religion – ideas that Zionists have fiercely debated.</p>

<p>During the early decades of the Zionist movement, for example, <a href="https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/political-zionism">political Zionists</a> emphasized the need for Jewish statehood as a solution to <a href="https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/antisemitism-in-history-the-era-of-nationalism-1800-1918">rising European antisemitism</a>. <a href="https://doi.org/10.2979/israelstudies.19.2.1">Cultural Zionists</a>, on the other hand, sought a solution to increasing Jewish assimilation. They wanted to reinvigorate Jewish identity by having a Jewish homeland – not necessarily a state – where a modern Hebrew culture could be created and flourish.</p>

<p>There was even disagreement among Zionists over whether the historical “Land of Israel,” or “Eretz Yisrael” in Hebrew, had to be <a href="https://theconversation.com/almost-zion-remembering-a-short-lived-jewish-state-in-new-york-253534">the location for Jewish self-determination</a>. In 1903, for example, Theodor Herzl, <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/theodor-herzl">the founder of the Zionist movement</a>, supported the British government’s offer for Jews to <a href="https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/the-uganda-proposal-1903">settle in parts of East Africa</a> then under the control of the British Empire.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white formal portrait of a bearded man with his arms crossed." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=828&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=828&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=828&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1040&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1040&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759339/original/file-20260911-50-bfg31o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1040&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Herzl22.jpg">Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the 1920s and ’30s, some Zionists in Mandatory Palestine, a territory then under British administration, advocated for <a href="http://www.zionistarchives.org.il/en/AttheCZA/AdditionalArticles/Pages/BritShalom.aspx">a binational Jewish-Arab state</a>. It was not until 1942, as the Holocaust was underway in Nazi-occupied Europe, that the Zionist movement <a href="https://www.jvl.levit.dev/the-biltmore-conference-1942">officially declared</a> that it sought a Jewish state.</p>

<p>After Israel’s establishment in 1948, its first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion – a left-wing “<a href="https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/socialist-zionism">Labor Zionist</a>” – argued that <a href="https://bgh.org.il/en/quotes/">the mission of Zionism was not complete</a>. In his view, it still required the “in-gathering of the exiles”: the immigration of all Jews to Israel. For Ben-Gurion, the only true Zionists were those who chose to live in Israel, which is what many Israeli Jews continue to believe.</p>

<p>Most Jews living in wealthy Western democracies, however, have preferred to <a href="https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/jewish-population-by-country">stay where they are</a> and support Israel from afar. Their notion of Zionism, dubbed “<a href="https://www.jpost.com/opinion/article-752037">diaspora Zionism</a>,” has dispensed with the demand that Jews should live in Israel. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.sourcesjournal.org/articles/liberal-zionism-and-the-idea-of-the-idea">liberal Zionism</a> that remains popular in the Jewish diaspora, at least among older Jews, has little in common with the <a href="https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/revisionist-zionism">revisionist Zionism</a> of right-wing Israeli leaders <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/18/opinion/benjamin-netanyahu-israel.html">like Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu</a>, which is committed to maintaining Israeli control over the entire West Bank. </p>

<p>Liberal Zionism shares even less with the religiously inspired <a href="https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/radical-messianic-zionism">messianic Zionism of extremist Jewish settlers</a> in the West Bank, or the <a href="https://religionmediacentre.org.uk/factsheets/factsheet-christian-zionism/">Christian Zionism</a> of evangelical Protestants, such as current <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/why-american-evangelical-christians-have-deep-ties-to-supporting-israel">U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee</a>. For these religious Zionists, whether Jewish or Christian, Zionism involves the fulfillment of God’s wishes, which they believe requires Jewish sovereignty over all of the biblical Land of Israel.</p>

<h2>Zionism as Israel’s actions</h2>

<p>What “Zionism” means, therefore, has never been definitively settled. It has always been contested by Zionists themselves, who are divided into different streams. Although there is less ideological diversity among Zionists today than in the prestate period, there are still deep disagreements, particularly between <a href="https://www.jpost.com/opinion/article-742927">religious and secular Zionists</a>.</p>

<p>Moreover, Zionism is more than an ideology. In the eyes of Zionism’s critics, it is what the Israeli state does in its name.</p>

<p>This is how Palestinians tend to think of Zionism. For them, Zionism is defined <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/466405">in terms of its outcomes for Palestinians</a>, which have included <a href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/journal/feature/generations-palestinian-refugees-face-protracted-displacement-and-dispossession">displacement, dispossession</a>, <a href="https://www.palestine-studies.org/en/node/1649445">destruction</a> and the <a href="https://www.hrw.org/report/2019/12/17/born-without-civil-rights/israels-use-draconian-military-orders-repress">denial of their rights</a>. This is why Palestinians and many of their supporters adamantly oppose it.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the minds of most Jews, by contrast, historically <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/01/opinion/zionism-jewish-israel.html">Zionism in practice has meant</a> Jewish liberation and sovereignty, a safe haven from persecution, a revival of the Hebrew language, and a renewed sense of collective pride, especially after the Holocaust.</p>

<p>These clashing ways of understanding Zionism help explain why it has become one of the most <a href="https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2024-05-22/zionism-disagreement-over-a-word-in-use-for-125-years">hotly contested terms</a> in today’s political vocabulary. <blockquote>
<p><strong>Why do people speak while they are sleeping? – Mubina, age 15, Uzbekistan</strong></p>
</blockquote>

<hr>

<p>Everyone sleeps, but not everyone understands much about sleep. One of my favorite parts of being a sleep psychologist is that when people hear what my job is, they always have tons of questions, like why do we need to sleep? Why do we dream? Do dogs dream? I get that one a lot, and the <a href="https://www.akc.org/expert-advice/training/what-do-dogs-dream-about/">answer is yes</a>!</p>

<p>Sometimes people want to chat about their sibling they share a room with who mumbles nonsense out loud all night long. Or maybe they’ve been teased themselves after delivering a complete but one-sided conversation while fully asleep at a slumber party.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=dIcnUcoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">I’ve studied sleep</a> for almost two decades, and I’m still not tired of discussing different aspects of it, especially what are called parasomnias: things your body does or your mind goes through while you’re asleep, such as nightmares, sleepwalking or talking in your sleep. Most are common and completely harmless; they only count as a disorder when they happen so often that they cause real problems.</p>

<h2>What’s happening while you’re asleep</h2>

<p>Sleep is not one single thing; you go through <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK19956/">several stages of sleep</a> every night.</p>

<p>About a quarter of your sleep is what’s called <a href="https://www.thensf.org/what-is-rem-sleep/">REM sleep</a>, short for rapid eye movement. This is the stage when most dreams, especially the vivid ones, happen.</p>

<p>Non-REM sleep, which includes the deeper stages of sleep, usually takes up between 75% and 80% of your night. It is an important stage of sleep where your body really throttles down, allowing it to rest and repair itself.</p>

<p>Doctors refer to these stages all together as your sleep architecture. People go through cycles of these stages roughly every 90 minutes each night. Non-REM sleep makes up more of your sleep right after bedtime, and then REM becomes a higher proportion of sleep in the early morning hours.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2008.02.001">All mammals</a>, from mice to cats to elephants, appear to sleep in some form or another. Researchers have found sleep is important for many things. When you’re asleep is when a lot of your <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/memory-consolidation">memories get strengthened</a> so they’ll last long term. Sleep is when <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-3476(96)70008-2">growth typically happens</a> in kids, and it is one of the times <a href="https://doi.org/10.1152/physrev.00010.2018">when your immune system is most active</a>.</p>

<p>Sleep is an important time for your brain and body to recharge and take care of themselves. Doctors recommend that <a href="https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.5866">teens get 8-10 hours</a> of sleep per night, and even more for younger kids: 10-13 hours for little kids ages 3-5, and 9-12 hours for bigger kids ages 6-12. </p>

<h2>Talking out loud while you’re asleep</h2>

<p>Even though someone who is asleep may look pretty much shut down for the night, their brain is not turned off. Different parts of the brain are active doing different things during different parts of the night.</p>

<p>Scientists think that sleeptalking happens when the parts of the brain responsible for language and speech are active while other parts of the brain that would typically <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsag123">prevent your mouth from physically talking</a> are asleep. </p>

<p>For the most part, sleeptalking is not even words. Usually it’s mumbles, laughs or whispers. If a sleeptalker does use language, it is most commonly the word “no” – that’s about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsx159">5% of all words that are said while asleep</a>. If the sleeptalker is saying words, they’re often questions and sometimes profanity. Rarely are the things sleeptalkers say polite, and often it sounds like they’re having a conflict with someone.</p>

<p>Sometimes it can sound like the sleeptalker is having a real conversation, pausing to allow the other person to speak – even if there’s no one else in the room. Researchers suspect you might be overhearing <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/00005053-197012000-00003">one side of a verbal exchange</a> from a sleeptalker’s dream. What a sleeptalker is saying out loud during REM sleep matches what they’re dreaming about at that moment about 80% of the time, according to studies in sleep labs.</p>

          </figure>

<p>You may be able to actually interact with someone who is sleeptalking; researchers have found that roughly half the time a sleeptalker will <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsae272">respond to a spoken question or statement</a>. But don’t get excited that you can get someone to spill their secrets or reveal something they don’t want to. There’s no scientific evidence of this happening.</p>

<p>There is not a ton of research on sleeptalking yet, but it appears that this phenomenon can happen <a href="https://sleepeducation.org/sleep-disorders/sleep-talking/">in any stage of sleep</a>. Studies do suggest there are differences between the sleep of people who sleeptalk and those who don’t. For instance, one study found that sleeptalkers get more than an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsab284">hour and a half less sleep per night</a> and roughly half as much REM sleep as nonsleeptalkers.</p>

<h2>Why do people talk in their sleep?</h2>

<p>The best explanation we have for sleeptalking is that the brain does not fall asleep all at once, and for some people the areas responsible for sleep remain active longer than the parts that help keep them quiet.  </p>

<p>This phenomenon is fairly common, with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sleep.2010.07.011">over two-thirds of people sleeptalking</a> at one time or another. It isn’t something to be concerned about if it has happened to you, though it does increase your likelihood of experiencing other parasomnias such as sleepwalking.</p>

<p>Sleeptalking is far more common in childhood. Researchers don’t fully understand why, but we do know that children have more of what’s called slow-wave non-REM sleep. The proportion of slow-wave sleep you have each night <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/27.7.1255">declines as you grow older</a>, so it is possible that less sleeptalking comes with this change in sleep architecture. </p>

<p>Looking at the big picture, sleeptalking is considered normal. But if you’re bothered by it – or by other parasomnias, such as sleepwalking, night terrors or bed-wetting – remember, they all become less common as you grow up. And there are treatments you can get from a sleep psychologist like me.</p>

<p>One last tip: Scientists do know that sleeptalking, as well as several other parasomnias, is more common when you’re overtired. So, the next time you talk in your sleep, you’ll know that it’s nothing to worry about, but perhaps a sign that you need to catch up on some extra zzz’s when you can.</p>
