title: What an AI “slowdown” could look like
excerpt: Demonstrators rally during a protest outside Anthropic headquarters in San Francisco, California, on July 11, 2026. | Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images Thi
body: Demonstrators rally during a protest outside Anthropic headquarters in San Francisco, California, on July 11, 2026. | Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

If you’d asked me yesterday what Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders had in common, I might have said “white hair.” But after a wild week in which AI doomerism burst solidly into the mainstream, the right-wing provocateur and progressive senator are joining forces — with various religious leaders, lawmakers, and the actor Joseph Gordon-Levitt, no less — to express their deep concern about AI regulation .  Concern about cutting-edge AI models had been mounting for months as those models increasingly behaved in ways their makers didn’t expect

It exploded last week, when a researcher at the AI company Anthropic resigned publicly and warned that the people building AI “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Do you have questions about this week’s AI panic? Candidly: me too! Submit your questions about AI safety and regulation through this form , and I’ll hunt down the answers for an upcoming edition

But it’s not a fringe position : Over the weekend, leading AI researchers and executives also warned that AI is developing dangerously fast and called for measures to rein it in. (We’ll run through those options in just a minute.) Now, a wide spectrum of lawmakers, activists, and pundits are also calling for stronger safeguards — Sanders and Bannon among them
The pair will speak at an event billed as a “Pro-Human Assembly” in Washington on Tuesday alongside Republican Sen
Marsha Blackburn, Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar, and the archbishop of San Francisco, among others

But President Donald Trump is decidedly not on board , and it’s hard to see how any substantive AI regulations could pass without him.  “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers,” he wrote this morning on Truth Social, “and the only one happy about it is China.” Go a little deeper How could the federal government make AI safer, if it could ever muster the bipartisan political will to act? My colleague Andrew Prokop recently put this question to a bunch of AI safety advocates and legal experts , and landed on three approaches:  Ban AI altogether

Federal law could hypothetically bar the development of AI systems that exceed human performance, or pause work on those systems until the government can stand up a new agency to monitor them.    Empower auditors
Some third-party authority — whether a government agency, a nonprofit technical organization, or an industry group — could begin reviewing AI systems before they go into public use
The Trump administration does a version of this already, but the process is voluntary and highly secretive
And it’s not clear if the officials reviewing these systems are super tech-savvy themselves.    Up the stakes
Congress could hold AI companies accountable for any harm that their systems or agents cause through changes to federal liability law

The threat of a huge, potentially bankrupting lawsuit could prompt those companies to be more cautious.  All three approaches have precedent in federal regulation, so they wouldn’t be (at least in theory) too tricky to stand up
The real roadblock, as always, is political
One AI researcher told Vox he worries we’ll miss the opportunity to regulate AI while waiting for lawmakers to get on the same page
Even under threat of apocalypse, Washington, DC, moves far, far slower than Silicon Valley.  One link for later ➨ Don’t skip leg day
Experts recommend that healthy adults incorporate strength training into their schedules at least twice a week

It builds strength, confidence, and body awareness, and can help preserve muscle mass and bone density as you age.  Before you go… Did you know… that 93,000 wild horses still roam the Western US ? They’re descended from animals introduced by European colonists in the 1500s.  Today’s trivia: What pro hockey player went on to found a major restaurant chain with locations across Canada and the US? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you which country voted against restarting membership talks with the European Union this year
That would be Iceland, where control over the country’s fisheries has been a major barrier to EU accession.

title: Why you should start planning for the holidays now. Yes — in September.
excerpt: The weather forecast might still be screaming “summer,” but the calendar betrays the truth: The holidays are going to be here before you know it
body: The weather forecast might still be screaming “summer,” but the calendar betrays the truth: The holidays are going to be here before you know it
What’s usually billed as a jolly time of year can inspire dread — all the planning, all the spending, all the gathering can be exhausting, especially if you have a large family
Of course you’d like to put that off for as long as possible, right? Surely these conversations can wait until after Halloween
But waiting too long can actually make the holidays more stressful — and can put undue stress on the women in your life, who often shoulder the burden of organizing and planning
One lollygagger who delays in committing to a plan can prevent the rest of the family from booking flights or buying necessary supplies

What can seem like an annoying text from your sister reminding you to RSVP for Thanksgiving in early October only adds to her mental load in planning a dinner for 20 people. “There can be an enormous amount of invisible labor involved in making the holiday magic happen, and that labor falls disproportionately on women and caregivers,” Jamila E

Holcomb , a licensed marriage and family therapist and associate teaching professor at Florida State University, told Vox. “If one person is coordinating everyone’s flights, planning meals, buying gifts, arranging childcare, communicating schedules, and managing family conflict, this can cause significant stress
It also makes one person responsible for everyone else’s experience, which is an unequal division of labor.” The pressure to plan the “perfect” holiday isn’t merely logistical
In our hyper-connected and visible culture, people may feel pressured to orchestrate a high-stakes production that somehow is meaningful, memorable, and Instagram-worthy
In other words, planning for the holidays can be its own form of labor these days

To help make the whole ordeal more manageable for everyone — not just the hosts or Type A family members — five experts offered their advice on sharing responsibilities and actually enjoying the season
Getting ahead of this coordination can help minimize the stress on everyone in a few months
So even though end-of-year celebrations might be the furthest thing from your mind, the ideal time to start planning them is, I’m sorry to say, right now
Here’s why early fall is the ideal time to start bugging the family group chat about the holidays
Planning early will save you money Prices on many goods, from flights to groceries , have increased over the last year
Getting ahead of these purchases before holiday crunch time can help you secure the best price and budget
While there’s no exact date for when to find the cheapest flights, travelers shouldn’t wait to book their tickets believing the price of gas will come down, travel expert Katy Nastro told Vox

In general, Nastro suggested locking in domestic travel between three and seven months ahead of time and between four and 10 months before international flights. “If you can get everything set… by the end of September for Thanksgiving, you’re going to be in a better place than most people,” Nastro said
The same goes for rental cars: reserve them now
Unlike flights, you don’t need to pay for them in advance, so you can always cancel the reservation if your plans change

Nastro recommends the platform AutoSlash , which aggregates prices from multiple rental companies. “With rental cars, there’s only so much inventory and you want to even make sure that you have that option if you need it,” she said
Early fall is also a great time to start shopping for presents, especially if you’re on a tight budget or coordinating a group gift with multiple people
Content creator and actor Rachel Ann Thomas and her eight siblings begin brainstorming ideas for their parents’ holiday gift in September or October every year
Christmas” Devereux decided to buy his loved ones matching Christmas pajamas, he started tracking down everyone’s sizes and placed the order before November

The earlier you nail down your shopping list, the sooner you can start looking for sales and slowly making purchases to save your bank account in December and avoid the stress of paying express shipping on last-minute gifts
You need time to create new traditions and to split the labor of creating them The holidays tend to be a period of nostalgia, and some families may heavily rely on time-honored traditions
But if you’ve outgrown them or just want to try something different, now is the best time to determine what would be meaningful, fun, and low-stress
Maybe that’s changing the location of a celebration from a grandparent’s home to a cousin’s; maybe that’s going on a fabulous vacation
The sooner you start thinking about it (and then commit to it), the easier everything else will be
Holcomb, the therapist, suggested asking your loved ones now what they want the holiday to feel like, what traditions or events matter most, and what they realistically have the capacity for
You can also ask if there’s anything new or different they’d like to incorporate this year

Then you can come up with a game plan for how to share planning responsibilities. “Our cultural expectations around the holidays can make it easy to confuse a ‘successful’ holiday with a highly productive one,” Holcomb said. “Making time to ask these questions is especially important because we can disrupt traditional relational patterns and roles that we have taken for granted as normal.” Both Holcomb and Thomas recommend creating a shared calendar or spreadsheet to keep track of logistics and divide responsibilities

In Thomas’s family, it’s called the Thomas Christmas Itinerary, and her mother starts it every September. “It basically lays out what the itinerary is for the whole Christmas time,” Thomas said. “What activities we’re doing, when we’re going over to grandparents’ houses, even down to what our dinner menus are.” A spreadsheet can also be helpful for assigning and delegating tasks so that one person doesn’t end up managing everything by default as things come together at the last minute

So once you’ve committed to a general plan with your family, start breaking things down further — and proactively ask people to take ownership of different events and tasks (e.g., choosing a movie to take all the kids to see together, buying the snacks, and figuring out who is driving everyone). “If you’re hosting, you don’t have to simultaneously be the chef, activities director, chauffeur, mediator, and person responsible for everyone’s enjoyment,” Holcomb said

Advance planning allows for the downtime everyone craves When you are able to take a broad view of the holidays without the time crunch, you can be more deliberate with the itinerary and build in breaks

Events can be planned with intention, not obligation, and you’ll be able to zoom out and see that your calendar is getting overloaded before you’re completely underwater. “Another priority should be adding rest into the schedule before you need it,” Emily Barry, the senior vice president of holiday planning at online stationery and art marketplace Minted , told Vox. “Protect mornings or evenings when nothing is planned

Give yourself permission to stay inside instead of attending another event.” “Don’t try to make the schedule perfect — make it meaningful,” Barry said. “Pick the one or two moments that are most important for everyone to be together, and build the rest of the holiday around those anchors.” Slow planning over the course of a month or two ultimately makes it easier to offer flexibility to family members who may have traveled a considerable distance, have young kids, or are juggling multiple celebrations, Barry said — and to be realistic about what you personally can handle. “The goal is to spend meaningful time together, not create an itinerary that everyone has to execute perfectly,” she said.

title: The 2020 election deniers running in swing states
excerpt: President Donald Trump has spent years making false claims about election fraud, including his refusal to accept that he lost the 2020 presidential election to
body: President Donald Trump has spent years making false claims about election fraud, including his refusal to accept that he lost the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden

Since that election, Republicans who denied or questioned the results have taken positions on local election boards, worked inside election offices, trained poll observers, and sought to influence state election laws
Now, as we head into the 2026 midterm elections, candidates who have denied or questioned the results of the 2020 election are running for governor and other powerful positions in key swing states
If elected, some could play important roles in overseeing future elections

Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Andrew Kaczynski, senior reporter at CNN who has been reporting on election-denying candidates and what their victories could mean for future elections
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

Which swing states are having elections featuring candidates who have denied the 2020 election results? The interesting thing is that we talked about in this article that we did on the five most key swing states is governor’s races
We’re talking Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin and Georgia
These are all states that Trump won in 2016, Biden in 2020, then Trump in 2024
And what we had talked about was how in each of these states, there are candidates running for governor who in four of the cases just outright denied the results of the 2020 election

How are these candidates in these five races faring? Does it look good for any of them? With the caveat that we’ve seen some pretty big polling misses already in two of these states, most of these candidates are behind in the polls, but there’s always the caveat that these are states that Trump won in 2024 and 2016
So they’re going to be, they’re true battlegrounds

And how much is their dispute or lie about the 2020 election coming up in their races? Not a ton, but what we did see was when we did this story, pointing out that at least in four of the key states, these are candidates that outright denied the election
When we reached out to three of them, they immediately gave us statements saying they would accept whoever won in their states in 2028
They said that Biden did win in 2020.  So we’ve seen election denial is kind of a liability, it would seem for these candidates
Just to give you the example of Michigan, John James has been down by five or six in some of the polls
He was somebody who originally got elected in a swing seat in 2022 as a member of Congress after he had two failed Senate runs
And he was like, “Yeah, of course Biden won in 2020.” And then when he ran this time, he actually went the other direction when he maybe was trying to get Trump’s endorsement
There’s a rally where he said that Trump won Michigan three times, which obviously did not happen
So you have a situation where it is probably a liability

A couple of these candidates are running from him, but at least two of them, Andy Biggs and John James, didn’t say that Biden won in 2020, didn’t say they’d certify the winner, and didn’t really give us a comment at all on that
But three of them said they would certify the winner

Do you see this as part of a broader effort on the part of this administration, or the Republican Party more broadly, to sort of legitimize the Big Lie into our institutions, into even election administration, which there’s been lots of reporting about? Or is it just a coincidence? Are there so many election deniers now that, inevitably, some of them are going to be running for office in key battleground states? I think it’s more the latter
It was just so thoroughly embedded in the Republican Party in 2020 and Trump had such a stranglehold over the party
But in 2022, many of those big election denier proponents that he backed, they did lose
So I do think it’s more of a liability for these candidates, but
It’s also why Trump supports a lot of them.  We’ve got a lot of candidates who deny the results of the 2020 election running for office in 2026
We’ve got people who deny the results of the 2020 election administering our elections in various key battleground states
We’ve got the Supreme Court fighting with lower courts about what maps they can use
We’ve got the president trying to redraw the rules around mail-in voting
What do you think this all amounts to for President Trump? Is this about the midterms? Is this about 2028? Is this just a pastime of his? It’s a pastime
It all runs through the fact that he thinks, or is lying, that he won in 2020, and this is all just a part of it
It’s all part of the same delusions about mail-in voting or fraud, or this or that
There’s an example of Andy Biggs, who’s running for governor in Arizona
He was a huge, huge stop the steal proponent and he was like, The governor could have de-certified the results if they wanted to, and that couldn’t obviously happen
John James, who said it at a rally with Trump: He won Michigan three times
Trump likes the candidates who lie and say that he won in 2020
It’s just like a pastime of his trying to find this fraud that doesn’t — like, obviously it exists
Obviously people do commit voter fraud at very low levels, but never has it been shown that it ever is on a large scale or enough to change the election

title: The hidden $350 surcharge on American households
excerpt: Diesel fuel prices in the United States topped $6 a gallon for the first time ever. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images This story was originally published by Grist and i
body: Diesel fuel prices in the United States topped $6 a gallon for the first time ever. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration
Diesel prices hit an all-time high on last week

Then another, and another.  According to AAA, the average price of diesel as of September 10 stands at a staggering $5.98 — about $2.31 more than in late February, when the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran
The jump has been even higher in some states, such as California, where a gallon of diesel currently costs $7.91
Most Americans don’t buy diesel fuel, but they pay for it indirectly in so many ways
It powers the trucks and ships that move everything from milk to lumber, and the costs are embedded in the prices people see at stores
The last time consumers saw diesel prices climb to such heights was in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine and they hit $5.82 per gallon

This has sent prices soaring, and consumers are increasingly feeling the impact.  “Early on, much of the cost increase gets absorbed along the supply chain through existing freight contracts and retailer margins,” David Ortega, a professor of food economics and policy at Michigan State University,  told the Associated Press . “But as contracts reprice and fuel surcharges take hold, more of that cost makes its way to the grocery store.”  All told, the rising price of diesel has cost US consumers an additional $46 billion, or about $350 per household, according to a Brown University tracker

That’s slightly less than the impact of rising gasoline prices — at $55 billion — but the 61 percent jump in diesel prices has outpaced the 41 percent increase in gas. “Diesel right now is caught up in more of a geopolitical turmoil than gasoline,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, an app that lets consumers track fuel prices

In addition to the Iran war, Ukraine’s increasingly successful attacks on Russian oil refineries have also applied upward pressure.  “Russia is no longer supplying the global market,” said De Haan, and US refineries are already at full capacity, giving them little ability to pick up the slack

Domestic inventories are at their lowest level since 1982, according ​to data from the Energy Information Administration. “We’re entering a key period for diesel consumption with the lowest inventories on record for early September,” David Russell, global head of market strategy at the brokerage service TradeStation, told Reuters . “Farmers and truckers typically use more diesel in the ​autumn, which raises the stakes for the current crisis and increases the risk of sharper price increases.” Winter is likely to bring more problems
Because heating oil is also essentially diesel, the millions of US households that still rely on it can expect unprecedented bills

This comes as the Trump administration has threatened to eliminate the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program , which helps households afford their fuel bills. “If you’re in the Northeast, then this is much more burdensome than anywhere else in the country,” Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association,  told Axios . “Families are getting hit by both gasoline and heating oil.”  These surging costs are hitting consumers just before the midterm elections, when the economy is at the front of voters’ minds

Normally, fuel prices are a somewhat downstream factor in the voting calculus, but Kevin Book, head of research at energy consulting firm ClearView Energy Partners, told Axios that this year could be different. “In cold weather states — particularly those that rely on fuels other than natural gas,” he said. “It could be a very big deal.” Even if the wars in Iran and Ukraine were to end tomorrow, it would take weeks or months for fuel prices to come down and diesel supply to recover.  “After both of those are solved, then once the flow normalizes, that will start to help global inventories recover,” De Haan said. “Only after inventories have recovered do diesel prices really see a full decline.”

title: How to be an ethical gossip
excerpt: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
body: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave
I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond
Please  send in  any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have
When I get together with my two best friends, we often talk about other people
We catch up on what acquaintances we knew in college are doing, and gossip about the mistakes people are making in their love lives
The other day I realized I left dinner and we had spent the entire time gossiping
Are we mean? Is it okay to gossip so much? It’s so much fun… Dear Dirt Disher, I share your love of gossip

I could blame my job ( I’m a journalist, of course I’m hungry for information ), but the truth is that I’ve always wanted to know what other people are up to.  At times, I have, like you, confronted the fact that gossip is often considered a vice
There was even once a medieval punishment for gossiping called a gossip bridle, an iron muzzle placed over the head of a person who spoke a little too freely

Those punitive dynamics were gendered, of course: Most of the gossip bridle’s victims were women, meaning that the directive to watch what you say may have really been a way to produce the right kinds of femininity

If you tried to avoid gossip, would you be a much better person, or just a quieter one?  To your question, then: If gossip feels good, can it really be all that bad? And to take it a step further: Is it possible that there could be something good about gossip itself, even though we’re taught that it’s bad? Either way, we still need to ask ourselves a few critical questions: How does the gossip we’re sharing affect the people we’re gossiping about? And how does it shape our relationships to the people we’re gossiping with? Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions

Sign up here! Cécile Fabre, a philosopher at the University of Oxford, took up the question of gossip in a 2023 paper , considering it through a framework drawn from Immanuel Kant’s moral philosophy, which holds that you must treat others as ends in themselves — rational beings deserving of respect — rather than as means to ends of one’s own

Fabre acknowledges that gossip can bring people together, as it does for you and your friends, but she also stresses that it has a darker side. “It lubricates and wrecks social relationships,” she writes.  First, Fabre distinguishes between good and bad gossip. “Good gossip” is truthful, and shared without breaking a promise to someone else by sharing it
If you’re telling lies about another person, or if you swore that you would keep a secret and are passing it on, gossiping raises other moral issues

But if you’re, say, passing along an anecdote that a mutual acquaintance freely and openly shared about a disastrous first date, you’re more likely to be in the clear.   But Fabre’s conclusion may make you uncomfortable: She argues that gossip is wrong when it leads us to deny others “the concern and respect which we owe them as persons.” As Fabre suggests, gossip is definitionally about people, but it often goes wrong precisely because it leads us to treat them with less dignity than we would accord to ourselves in our own personhood

For Fabre (and perhaps also for Kant, who never took the question up explicitly), then, gossiping is morally wrong when it uses others for entertainment or otherwise denigrates them to make oneself feel superior.    It’s possible that Kant, whose moral laws aspired to the universal, would have been even more draconian than Fabre makes him out to be
But as his own life demonstrates, things can get fuzzier in practice

The great metaphysician of morals was himself known to love a good gossip session over wine at a dinner party, and, according to his book of lectures, Anthropology from a Pragmatic Point of View , he thought that this habit was fine, as long as no one divulged what was said later.  In the centuries since Kant let stories slosh over the edge of his cup, plenty of other thinkers have become apologists for gossip, arguing that it’s an unavoidable and necessary aspect of social life
Anthropologist Robin Dunbar claims in Grooming, Gossip, and the Evolution of Language that gossip was key to our survival as a species
When ancient hominids gossiped, they were sharing information about dangerous people and practices, while also maintaining social order
Gossip was a form of cultural learning, and it easily spread knowledge across a group

Dunbar has more recently suggested that 85 percent of everyone’s conversations are dedicated to talking about social matters, much of which could be considered gossip.  Some feminist philosophers, among them Karen Adkins, author of Gossip, Epistemology, and Power: Knowledge Underground , have maintained that gossip can be a tool of the disenfranchised. (Think again about whose mouths were sealed by the gossip bridle and ask yourself who ordered them shut.) Whisper networks can inform people about bad working environments or abusive bosses
That, in turn, builds trust among the disempowered, which can be a path back to power.  It doesn’t, however, sound like that’s exactly what you and your besties are up to
It may be true that talking about people who aren’t there helps you sustain your sense of intimacy with your pals who are
But in Kantian terms, that might also mean that you’re effectively treating those absent others as means to ends that have nothing to do with them
And what should we call that if not disrespect? You mentioned two different kinds of gossip in your question: swapping information about former college classmates and dissecting people’s love lives
You might spend some time breaking those categories down further to figure out what kind of gossip you and your friends are engaging in
In a large study on gossip, psychologists found that most gossip was not actually malicious or dedicated to criticizing other people; the majority was neutral
If, on reflection, you find your gossip is predominantly unkind, you might want to pull back
Not because all gossip is inherently wrong, but because being overly malicious could, as a different philosopher suggests, shape your experience of the world for the worse
Here, I’m thinking about the 20th-century existential philosopher Martin Buber, who offers a nuanced account of how we treat others that might shape our understanding of gossip
In 1923, in his book I and Thou, he identifies two modes through which you can interact with the world

In the I-it mode, you encounter individuals as objects, or “its.” By contrast, an I-thou encounter treats everything you meet, whether it’s a person or a tree, as an entity with which you can enter into a relationship
Buber thought the I-thou attitude was a fundamentally human capacity
It describes the ability to relate to others, and have a dynamic emerge between you — rather than just objectify them
While Kant helped inspire Buber, I prefer the latter’s quasi-spiritual take not just about right and wrong, but what we lose out on

When we gossip too much, we may take on an I-it attitude to others, and forget that they are living and breathing people with whom we have relationships, people who are struggling to make choices of their own, and people who, like us, sometimes get it wrong.  I’m ultimately less concerned that you gossip at all than I am about your observation that the entirety of your social interactions are dedicated to gossip, with little room for other topics
I worry that you and your friends aren’t making room for sharing your own interests or your own struggles
In that sense, the issue might not be that you’re disrespecting people who aren’t there, but rather that you’re not in true dialogue with the people who are present

title: How to find a date in real life
excerpt: If you want to hear someone complain, one of your best bets is to ask one of your single friends what the dating landscape is like right now
body: If you want to hear someone complain, one of your best bets is to ask one of your single friends what the dating landscape is like right now
You’ll hear tales of first dates that lead nowhere, conversations that feel like they were ripped from a social media feed, and more and more people resigning themselves to partnerless existence
Even what once seemed like an ever-flowing fount of new romantic possibilities has now dried up: It feels like the days of meeting The One via a dating app are behind us

As dating coach Lily Womble explains: “Dating can be so exhausting, depleting, demoralizing, and I only think dating apps have increased that experience for single folks.” Despite how discouraging it can be, though, a lot of people still desire partnership

Womble is the author of Thank You, More Please: A Feminist Guide to Breaking Dumb Dating Rules and Finding Love , and she spoke with Vox about how to overcome dating fatigue. “If you do want to find love in a romantic partnership, there is a more healthful and empowering way to go about it that centers you as the main character,” she explains

So how do you center yourself? How do you take your dating life off of your phone and into the real world? We answer those questions and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Womble, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
If you’re used to dating apps and you want to meet someone in person, how do you make that happen? Dating in person is a lost art of social connection
I think that our reliance on dating apps has made us all sicker in some ways

They’re designed to keep you sitting there with a gallon bag full of quarters and a Big Gulp, hoping to pull the triple cherry and get lucky.  It’s really important to reset your brain [from] dating apps, to get in-person to build new connections
It is as simple and as complicated as three steps.  What are the steps? Number one: joy-building
You need to exit your house, get off your couch, and go do something in your town or city that brings you some amount of joy with other people.  It could be something free or something paid
The point is not to be in proximity to hotties at this event
The point is to make a new friendship, to make a new connection, to say, “Hey, how’s it going?” From there, you’re expanding your social circle
The function of a dating app is purely to expand your social circle and expand your opportunity window to meet somebody

Same with expanding your social circle with joy-building.  You never know which 70-year-old you meet at your quilting night in your small town, whose son’s boyfriend’s cousin comes to a party and suddenly you’ve met the love of your life
I went to an improv class, I made a friend that introduced me to her social circle, then I met Chris, my husband
Joy-building helps you meet the right people
Second, you’ve got co-conspiratorship: helping your friends help you better
Now, your friend might say, “I don’t know any single people.” To that, you say, “I don’t either
So let’s co-create creative solutions
You have a workplace, you have a work conference
Are you looking out for me there? Here’s the kind of person that I’m looking for
Here’s the questions I want you to ask somebody.”  Two of my clients were each other’s co-conspirators

That didn’t matter because one of them visited the other, and in the airport met an eligible man, asked the qualifying and disqualifying questions, found out he was single, that he was eligible, that he was a good fit, and set them up
So you need to have co-conspirators, you need to have friends looking out for you
Just like your friend asked you to be in their wedding, you need to ask them to support you in this way too
Finally, we’ve got flirting, which is the most vomitous, nerve-wracking part of this plan
The good news is that it’s a buildable skill set
It’s not just something that your favorite friend who is so naturally flirty has and you don’t
I think that flirting is essentially a joyful, courageous connection.  People overcomplicate flirting to be this game

But I really believe, and have seen in my own experience, that flirting is just simply approaching somebody, asking a genuine question, and seeing if that person wants to co-create a conversation with you
To see if it’s romantic, you just ask, “Hey, random question
So are you single?” All of this requires 10 seconds of courage to go up to somebody and say, “Hey, you’re cute

I just wanted to come tell you that.” One of my clients did that on a crosswalk with a man that she found cute and they ended up dating.  You make it sound so easy, but that joy-building, that getting out and talking to people, that can be really hard
One, it’s hard to be joyful when it feels like the world is falling apart around us
Also, some of us are more shy than others
And there are people who lost a lot of valuable flirt skill-building time during the pandemic
I hear you, but how do you do it?  We have lost a lot of social skills

Meroueh may have found a way to clean up steelmaking without driving up the price
